speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, following the closing of the Canada Games in Charlottetown, I feel honoured and proud to stand in the House and recognize all Canadian athletes who participated in the Canada Winter Games, 1991.
I am especially proud of our Prince Edward Island athletes for their fine performance. Prince Edward Island secured one gold medal in boxing, won by Mark Docherty, and three bronze medals, two won in boxing by Geriy Ryan and Trevor McAdam, and one bronze medal won in curling by the Sean Matheson foursome.
I wish to applaud all the organizers of the Canada Games, the thousands and thousands of volunteers who have established themselves as some of the most exceptional people in Canada.
I would also like to thank the Government of Prince Edward Island, the federal government, and specifically the Ministry of Youth, Fitness and Amateur Sport, for their efforts and support for the games.
Finally, I would like personally to commend each and every athlete who came, who participated, and who made this cultural and athletic event truly Canadian.
Yes, Canada, our youth are great. Yes, Canada, our athletes are competitive. Yes, Canada, we are a great nation.

Mr. Speaker, as you know, tourism is Ontario's second largest industry. This sector of the economy has suffered significant losses in the last two years. I therefore welcome the announcement by the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism that there will be an allocation of $4 million toward the promotion of southern Ontario as a tourist destination.
The southern Ontario advertising fund will be used to help tourist operators and other attractions throughout the region reach the American market in a way that will attract the most visitors. Instead of advertising against each other, they will be encouraged to co-operate and sell southern Ontario as a package.
In order for this plan to work, there must be co-operation and financial commitment from the province and the private sector. It is incumbent upon the province to make certain that it will commit the necessary funds toward revitalizing this important industry and take an active part in this effort.
I call upon the Government of Ontario and the region's private sector to give their enthusiastic support to this program in order that more tourists will view our region as an attractive destination.

Mr. Speaker, Earl Pratt and Ivan Morgan of Jamaica have been victims of violations of articles 14 and 7 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. Amnesty International and I appeal to the Human Rights Division at External Affairs to intervene on their behalf.
Pratt and Morgan are scheduled for execution tomorrow morning in Jamaica. It is Canada's obligation to uphold and strengthen human rights instruments and decisions.

March 6, 1991
Would the minister for the human rights branch of External Affairs move immediately and appeal to the Jamaican Minister of Foreign Affairs to prevent this execution?

Mr. Speaker, the Great Lakes pollution prevention initiative announced yesterday by the environment minister is a major step in the revitalization of the Great Lakes. As a member of Parliament representing Canadians living and working along Lake Erie, I am pleased that every sector will have input in developing strategies needed to achieve major reductions of toxic substances that are polluting the Great Lakes.
I am also pleased that funding will be available to assist industry in introducing pollution technologies into its operations. Prevention of pollution is the key for a cleaner environment for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, before the Empire Club and the Canadian Club in Toronto, the Minister of Finance said that "what we", the government, "are trying to do is break a cycle of wage and salary settlements that are 2 and 3 per cent-sometimes more-higher than inflation".
Last year the inflation rate was 5 per cent. I wondered what sector of the Canadian work force was receiving average annual wage increases of 7 per cent or 8 per cent.
Labour Canada says that private sector workers averaged a 5.7 per cent wage increase, public sector workers 5.9 per cent, and federal workers averaged only 5.3 per cent.
So who was getting 7 per cent or 8 per cent? Canada's executives, that is who: 7.8 per cent in Toronto, 7.3 per cent on average. A typical chief executive officer earns $450,000 a year.
The Minister of Finance would be better to target his friends on Bay Street, rather than to blame the workers on the shop floor for our current recession.
I hope the Minister of Finance sends a copy of his comments to the Governor of the Bank of Canada, whose salary has increased by as much as 21 per cent for each of the last three years.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I was profoundly disappointed and very frustrated by the press release the Quebec government issued yesterday afternoon on a joint decontamination program for abandoned sites presenting a high environmental risk.
Imagine my surprise, Mr. Speaker, when I noticed not one of the five sites proposed by Quebec was in the Abitibi-Temiscamingue region, where most contaminated sites are found. For instance, the Duparquet site was deemed a threat to the environment and a high risk site by the Quebec government.
Today, I made my profound displeasure known to Minister Pierre Paradis and to the hon. Robert de Cotret and I urged them to give priority, and the sooner the better, to the abandoned and dangerous contaminated sites in my region.

Mr. Speaker, consumers in Sudbury and Ottawa who filed numerous complaints with the Competition Bureau of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs over gasoline prices, cautiously welcome the news that the department has finally decided to take action and launch an investigation into possible gasoline price fixing in these two cities.
For several months, consumers from all across Canada have been suspicious of gas prices and the variety of reasons given for vast price differences throughout the country. The government, however, only promised to monitor the situation.
This investigation should have started earlier. Canadians deserve protection from being taken at the pumps. They want the government to assure them that gas prices

March 6, 1991

are indeed fair. It remains to be seen if this government can give such assurances.

Mr. Speaker, on November 2,1989, the Quebec Department of the Environment wrote the federal member of Parliament for Temiscamingue, Mr. Gabriel Desjardins, concerning contaminated sites called high risk abandoned sites. This letter mentioned sites in Amtfield, two in Duparquet, two more in Cadillac and one in Joutel.
Yesterday, the Quebec Minister of the Environment, Mr. Pierre Paradis, approved a federal-provincial decontamination agreement concerning high risk sites in Quebec which did not include these dangerous sites. And the sites covered under this agreement were those designated by Quebec!
Mr. Speaker, once again the Quebec Minister of the Environment forgot Northern Quebec in his prayer, and the people of Abitibi-Temiscamingue will end up in paradise, or in hell, because of these dangerous contaminated sites.

Mr. Speaker, the finance minister's latest budget is like 19th century literature: you have to read between the lines to understand its true meaning, for it is not what it says that is significant but, rather, what it does not.
Many communities in northern Ontario rely on either mining or lumber for their well-being. This government's high interest rate and high dollar policies have crippled these industries.
How is this budget going to help? By cutting back transfer payments and shifting an even greater burden to municipalities that have already been brutalized by the recession that the government created.
The Minister of Finance is forecasting an unemployment rate of 10 per cent. For most northern communities
the current rate is nearly twice that and is only expected to increase. How will this budget help the unemployed? By cutting $100 million from job retraining, by cutting social housing, health, and welfare. What does the budget say? Absolutely nothing.
For northern Ontario last year's budget, with its debilitating cutbacks, represented a Stephen King style massacre. This year's budget with its cryptic, silent approach is more along the lines of an Alfred Hitchcock terror; it just leaves one hanging.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance made interesting choices in his budget. For example, he chose to continue the business and entertainment tax deduction which cost $1.1 billion. In fact he made the deduction even better by extending the write-off to include the new goods and services tax. The Minister of Finance also chose to cut the federal contributions for health services by the same $1.1 billion.
Yet, here is what the Prime Minister said about health care in August 1983:
The Progressive Conservative Party is in favour of quality medicare,
universal medicare delivered to our citizens. Problems have arisen
because of a unilateral and arbitrary cutback by the federal
government to the provinces who are charged with footing the bill.
That's the problem.
Today Canadians want to know why the problem of 1983 has been greatly accelerated by the Prime Minister's own government. They want to know about the government's choices: the choice to attack medicare in order to protect the big businesses.

Mr. Speaker, President George Bush will be visiting Ottawa on March 13 and March 14 to sign the Canada-U.S. bilateral acid rain accord.
This accord commits both countries to permanently decrease acid rain-causing emissions to a level that will no longer threaten the Canadian environment.
The signing of the agreement on air quality between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States of America marks the culmination of a

March 6, 1991
long history of this government's efforts to find a solution to the problem of acid rain.
The air quality accord, plus the measures contained in the Canadian acid rain control program and the U.S. Clean Air Act, will control the acid rain problem and provide a means to resolve other transboundaiy air quality concerns such as urban smog and air toxics.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday it was announced that another 400 mining jobs would be lost in Elliot Lake within the next few months. This will raise the total number of mine jobs lost since last summer to nearly 3,000.
The resulting impact on local small business, the municipal government, school boards, and the community at large will be extensive, resulting in estimated job losses of 5,100 which is over 60 per cent of the labour force.
Elliot Lake and the neighbouring north shore communities are making the tremendous economic adjustments needed to continue as a thriving community.
However, the federal government must respond immediately in the following way: by approving the $6.3 million Community Futures budget, by providing a CMHC loan guarantee to ensure the viability of the retirement living project, by approving the funding for improved navigational aids at the Elliot Lake Airport, and by decentralizing federal government departments and agencies to Elliot Lake.
Elliot Lake has the spirit to survive this crisis, but the support of the federal government is crucial to its success.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to take this opportunity to express my concern about a matter that may have a serious impact on CN workers in Jonquiere. Let me explain, Mr. Speaker. For several months, CN and Roberval Saguenay have been discussing the possibility of letting Roberval Saguenay take charge of the transportation of goods in the Saguenay-Lac-Saint-Jean area. In itself, this may be a good deal for both parties. What worries me however, is that Roberval Saguenay, which is anxious to get a good deal, will come down heavily on CN workers. I have enough information to believe that the deal between CN and Roberval Saguenay would put about 30 CN workers out of work in our area.
Mr. Speaker, if the deal is closed on that basis, it would be entirely unacceptable. Roberval Saguenay must reject that option. I want to appeal to the directors of Roberval Saguenay and CN to inform our workers and our communities of the real tenor of current discussions, the various options considered and the real impact this will have on jobs.

Mr. Speaker, there is an old saying that if you have a glass that is half full, all the pessimist sees is a glass that is half empty. Well, if the glass contained 18,200 pounds of chlorine, federal transport regulations see a completely empty glass.
That is the lesson from an investigation into a derailment in February 1990 in Brampton, Ontario. At the time CN officials told local authorities that one of the cars, a damaged tanker, was empty, containing only the residue of a chlorine shipment that had already been removed. It was not until they began loading the tanker on to a flat-bed car that they found out it contained nine tonnes of deadly chlorine.
The investigation blames contradictory federal regulations. The resulting confusion could have been fatal both for railway and emergency workers and adjacent residents.
It is absolutely clear that the government has to move immediately to clear up this confusion. We cannot tolerate slipshod relations when the safety of Canadian workers and residents is at stake.
March 6, 1991

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister and concerns the Spicer Commission's total loss of credibility.
As we are nearing the debate on the Allaire report that will take place this weekend and the tabling of the Belanger-Campeau report, and at a time when several provinces have established parliamentary committees to examine the division of powers, why doesn't the Special Joint Committee of the Parliament of Canada have the right to examine the division of powers? Why is everybody across Canada examining this issue, except the Parliament of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, the Official Opposition in the Parliament of Canada has every right to advise us of its opinions in that respect. We have the Spicer Commission and we have the Beaudoin-Edwards Special Joint Committee which is now sitting. I am sure the various commissions and committees would be glad to receive the comments and recommendations of the Official Opposition.
If, at a given time, it appears appropriate for this House to create a parliamentary committee to examine the positions of the Official Opposition and other political groups, we will of course take steps to initiate this process.
However, as far as the negative comments on the Spicer Commission are concerned, I may remind the Leader of the Opposition that the Liberal Member for Gatineau-La Lievre, Mr. Assad said a few days ago that this was no time to complain about the Spicer Commission because they hadn't had a chance to do anything yet. So, listen to your member before complaining about the Spicer Commission.
Mr. Speaker, I think the public will be the judge of the credibility of the Spicer commission. I am concerned about the role of Parliament.

Oh, oh.
Oral Questions
Mr. Speaker. The hon. member.

I am very concerned about the limited role of Parliament at this crucial time in our country's history.
Many provinces are looking at the issue of division of powers, but the Prime Minister has tied the hands of the parliamentary committee when it comes to a full public examination of this issue.
However, the Prime Minister has set up a committee of deputy ministers in secret to study and overhaul the federal powers. Why are deputy ministers meeting, again behind closed doors, to review the division of powers but the public parliamentary committee is not allowed to look at the same issues?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says there is a limited opportunity for Parliament to examine this matter. I would be happy to hear from my hon. friend in regard to any suggestion that is reasonable and appropriate. I would be happy, as I have indicated, to undertake a dialogue which would give rise to a constructive discussion. I think the greater the input, the greater opportunity Canada will have to deal with this matter.
Perhaps my hon. friend could begin with the fact that the Official Opposition has nine Opposition Days in the House. Perhaps a good way to begin and to help the country might be for the opposition to take one of those days and set out with some clarity and some precision its ideas on how this might be accomplished.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are painfully aware that secret meetings and rolling the dice have cost us dearly.
What we want to know now from the Prime Minister of Canada is this: Is he prepared today to announce an expanded mandate for the parliamentary committee to look at the specific issue of division of powers so that the Government of Canada and the Parliament of Canada can have some say on this crucial issue as it is being examined by provinces across the country? Will I get an answer?

Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated in the past, the government leader in the House of Commons is ready to meet with the representatives of my hon. friend at any time, or with members of the NDP, to examine this possibility. If it is

Oral Questions
constructive and helpful, we would be happy to proceed with an instrument that could be of benefit to Canada.
My hon. friend refers to a comment I made in regard to rolling the dice, thereby attacking me.
Oh, oh.

Perhaps I could refer to a comment she made on June 4, quoted in The Toronto Star. "Said Copps: "Jean Chretien, you have not understood Quebec and you are gambling dangerously with the survival of Canada. One does not find the future, Jean, by looking in a rear view mirror".

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The Prime Minister wants Canadians to believe they are being listened to in advance of the national government taking any position on renewed federalism. If that is the case, why has the Prime Minister instructed a powerful committee of deputy ministers, operating in secret, behind closed doors, to draft proposals on renewed federalism?
I ask the Prime Minister, is the Spicer commission a genuine public consultation or a public diversion while the Prime Minister, once again, orchestrates matters behind closed doors?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend cannot have it both ways. On the one hand, he asks for public participation and when we bring forward the Spicer commission, he leads the attack to undermine and denigrate the commission.
The Spicer Commission is functioning with a view to receiving as many opinions from Canadians as is possible. I think all members of the Spicer commission look upon their responsibilities very seriously. They are earnestly seeking out as many opinions as they can to be helpful to Canada. The Edwards-Beaudoin committee will be sitting the next seven or eight days through western Canada, inviting submissions from Canadians in regard to the amending formula, which is veiy important. They will then go to Atlantic Canada, throughout Ontario and then throughout the Province of Quebec.
It is our hope that the substance of the Spicer commission, along with the procedural improvements that hopefully can be made as a result of the Beaudoin-Edwards committee, will help all parliamentarians along
as we put together a formula and a matter of substance that Canadians will view with favour as contributing an important building block to Canadian unity and the building of a new Canada of which all Canadians will be proud.

Mr. Speaker, I hope all Canadians have noted that the Prime Minister has twice refused to deal directly with a question about the secret committee of deputy ministers operating behind closed doors. The Prime Minister is playing his cards pretty close to his vest, but it will not hide the fact that, once again, he is playing poker with the future of Canada.
Is the Prime Minister prepared to tell members of this House and, through this House, all Canadians precisely what is the mandate of this committee of deputy ministers and when is the Prime Minister prepared to share that mandate and their findings with all Canadians? Is he going to do it now so that Canadians can comment, or is he only going to unveil this master plan later when the so-called public consultation is all finished?

Mr. Speaker, there seems to be a serious problem with this nefarious committee. If it is secret, how does the hon. member know about it?
Let me put the anxieties of my hon. friend to rest. There is no secret committee; but I can tell him that if there was one, I would ask him to join.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
The finance minister stated in his budget that he is discussing new fiscal arrangements with provincial and territorial counterparts. There is a growing concern that these new fiscal arrangements will fundamentally impact on national unity and on the future relationship of the federal government with the provinces and the territories.
I asked the Prime Minister yesterday and I ask him again today: In these discussions on "new fiscal arrangements", what is going to be on the table? Are health care, regional development and social programs going to
March 6, 1991

be on the table? Are these fiscal negotiations, in truth, in reality, constitutional negotiations by another name?

Mr. Speaker, these are not "constitutional negotiations by another name", to pick up my hon. friend's words. We have been having a number of discussions with the provinces over the past year or so on the question of equalization, a program which must be renewed in 1992, with the major transfers of Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan, as to what the structure of those two programs should be, as well as on the question of the tax collection agreements. These discussions will continue at least over the course of the next few months.
What I was announcing in the budget was a broadening of that process, to invite some public dialogue on the question of how these transfers should be structured and what the tax collection agreements might be revised to.
But I should underscore the point that the discussions do not involve any discussion of the medicare program, of post-secondary education, of highways development, where the moneys might be used by the provinces. Those are not within our jurisdiction; those are within the provincial jurisdictions.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary for the Prime Minister.
The finance minister included in his budget speech that he was going to be talking about these new fiscal arrangements. Everyone knows that fiscal arrangements are a key part of the constitutional make-up of this country, and they do affect health care, social programs and regional development.
It does seem that the government is seeking to change some of these arrangements, which is simply different men at a different table, similar to what we saw in the Meech Lake discussions.
I want to ask the Prime Minister again: Is he trying to have his government and his finance minister negotiate new fiscal arrangements which are really a discussion for constitutional arrangements? Is the Prime Minister allowing the finance minister to negotiate fundamental
Oral Questions
changes to Canadian federalism before the people of Canada have been heard?

Mr. Speaker, the answer to that question is, of course, no.
I am quite surprised by the almost pejorative allusion that the leader of the NDP makes to both Meech Lake and the process. Meech Lake was widely supported and indeed applauded by her predecessor as leader of the NDP and almost every member of Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister, and it is quite straighforward. Does this government intend to negotiate fiscal arrangements which actually concern the Constitution more than anything else? Are those social programs, those national health programs on the table? The Prime Minister must be honest with Canadians. What is on the table?

Mr. Speaker, the answer is the same in English and in French. I just gave the answer in English. There are no negotiations on fiscal arrangements or social programs. It was clear in English and it is clear in French.

Mr. Speaker, for seven budgets the Minister of Finance has promised us that the Canadian economy would be more competitive.
In just two short years, Canada has lost 229,000 or 11 per cent of all our manufacturing jobs. This government is presiding over the deindustrialization of Canada.
Today, 1,300,000 Canadians have no jobs and the minister has promised that another 200,000 Canadians will lose their jobs. Just how far is this government prepared to go in deindustrializing Canada?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend, in his most cataclysmic tones, deplores the fact as we do that 211,000 jobs have been lost during the recession.
In this morning's Financial Post a result of a study by the Canada West Foundation, indicates that in the last

March 6, 1991
Oral Questions
recession when my hon. friend was a member of the government, 300,000 jobs were lost in the same sector.
My hon. friend never once rose to protest that fact against the government of which he was a member.
There were lay-offs.
"There were lay-offs", he says. When you lose your job when the Liberals are in office, it is a lay-off.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friend knows full well that the recession is a serious one, that indeed there were 140,000 jobs lost in the last two months in the private sector in Canada, but interest rates have come down some 408 basis points since their high of last spring.
Investment intentions appear to be strong. Confidence is returning to the country as interest rates continue to drop, and the Minister of Finance has laid out a program for growth and economic prosperity which we believe will begin to bite in the middle of this summer. It will bring great advantages to all parts of the country.

Mr. Speaker, if the Prime Minister is saying that the loss of all of these manufacturing jobs is justified by something that happened many years ago, then this is what we are seeing from this government.
You cannot build an economic future for Canada on empty rhetoric.
This was a Prime Minister who promised Canadians jobs, jobs, jobs-but he delivered them to the Americans.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, when will this government realize that we will not be able to compete tomorrow unless we invest today in our young Canadians, in science and technology, and in research and development? Will the government commit today to make these critical investments in our future so that the jobs and the hopes of a generation of young Canadians will stop moving south?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is quite right when he talks about the need for greater competitiveness and the
availability of better jobs. This is why some of the difficult structural changes that we have introduced, that have met with ferocious opposition from some of the protectionist comers of Canada-like the goods and services tax and the free trade agreement-are bringing about and will restructure the Canadian economy and render it much more competitive, and thereby bring benefits to Canadians.
For example, in the report to which I have referred, prepared by the Canada West Foundation, since the free trade agreement was introduced-and I quote directly from the report this morning- "Canada increased high-tech exports by $4 billion since the deal, while such imports from the United States fell by $600 million."
Hear, hear.

"In most sectors, bilateral trade levels were unchanged but Canadians exported more electrical machinery, aerospace, railway rolling stock, scientific professional instruments, special trade transactions, zinc and zinc products, precision metals and stones, et cetera to the United States. This indicates that a structural reform such as the free trade agreement is improving our competitiveness, enhancing our productivity-"
We have lost 229,000 manufacturing jobs.
-which is still not appropriate, but we are going the right way and we will pick up those job losses as we come out of the recession.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The Minister of the Environment told us that yesterday's announcement on the clean-up of the Great Lakes was in line with his Green Plan. Unfortunately, he was right: it was merely an exercise in public relations. For the clean-up plan to work, it must be carried out in consultation with the municipalities and provinces involved. My question is this: Is this another green balloon? Why did he make his announcement before finalizing the plan or consulting with the provinces and municipalities involved?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find the hon. member's question incredible. Yesterday, the Minister of the Environment announced a substantial clean-up plan for the Great Lakes, a plan that provides $25 million for the development of a strategy and for setting up a centre to fight pollution. The plan will be implemented with the co-operation of the industry and other levels of government. Therefore, I think the hon. member should rise to show his support for this government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the parliamentary secretary. Now I know why we have not had any meetings on C-78. The plan contained no targets. It had no programs.
At 10 o'clock yesterday morning the minister stated unequivocally that the goal of zero discharge, which every environmentalist wants to see and which is crucial if the plan is going to succeed, was absolutely scientifically impossible to attain. Subsequently, after lunch, and after a great deal of pressure on that, he suddenly reversed his position and said that the government's goal was zero discharge.
Will the parliamentary secretary please share with this House the scientific breakthroughs that occurred in those two hours?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I can share with this House is the fact that the issue of virtual elimination or zero discharge is far more complex than the hon. member would suggest in his question. I can indicate to the House that this government has a plan in place which includes a provision for zero discharge for eight chemicals which have already been identified. In other words, in the case of mirex and several other chemicals, the manufacturing, the use, the importation and the exportation is not allowed, in short it is zero discharge.
I would also note in the new pulp and paper regulations which are coming into place that there will be the virtual elimination of dioxins and furans, as I think all members of this House would wish.
Oral Questions
In the third case, the example in the mining industry, heavy metals such as in liquid effluents like copper and nickel, are being controlled to a level that is sufficient to protect the environment.
This strategy is consistent with the green plan. It is consistent with the kind of feedback that we got from Canadians in the largest consultation process that ever occurred in the history of this country. It is indeed the kind of strategy which will ensure that the environment for our children and our grandchildren will be protected, unlike any kind of policy which that party had in place when it was in power.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of the Environment, I put my question to the Prime Minister. Yesterday, the Minister of the Environment doled out the next instalment of the green plan slush fund by announcing a $25 million public relations Great Lakes fund.
Canada agreed 13 years ago to a zero discharge of toxics into the Great Lakes. Under Canada's Environmental Protection Act the government has the power to act.
Will the government announce today a federally enforced ban on all toxic substances going into the Great Lakes?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, what I can do is read to the hon. member and to interested members the list of those substances which already are banned for which there is indeed zero discharge: mirex, polybrominated biphenyls, polychlorinated terphenyls, alachlor, lepto-phos, phosphamidon-there are times like this when I wish I was a chemist rather than an historian-cyhexatin and 2, 3, 4, 5-bis (2-butylene) tetrahydro-2-furfural. Those are all at present under the zero discharge regulations to which the hon. member referred.
Let me also include, Mr. Speaker, a statement from the agreement to which the hon. member refers, which is the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement of November 1987, in which it states under Article 2, Purposes, Part A: "The discharge of toxic substances and toxic amounts be prohibited and the discharge of any or all persistent toxic substances be virtually eliminated".

March 6, 1991
Oral Questions
That is the same terminology which the minister used yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary for the Prime Minister. In December, the green plan promised to almost double funding for energy conservation and alternatives. But last week the energy, mines and resources estimates cut funding for energy efficiency and alternatives for the seventh year in a row.
My question to the Prime Minister is: How does the government plan to restore the promised funding and thus avoid the impression of deceitful opportunism?

speakeroldname: Mr. John A. MacDougall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if you are a socialist in this country, you spend. If you want to deal with the reality, you work in co-operation with the industry, with the provinces and with the federal government. This is what this government is doing.
We are doing our utmost to co-operate and work with all on a future energy policy that will be unique for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister.
For the last four years, we have all witnessed rampant sawmill closures, causing thousands and thousands of layoffs across Canada. The Canadian Lumbermen's Association puts the blame for this squarely on the softwood lumber export tax. The Canadian high dollar also serves to aggravate the situation. Lumber exports to the U.S. are practically nil.
Will the Prime Minister, in his meeting with President Bush next week, indicate to him that Canada is planning to cancel the softwood lumber agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. gentleman should know if he reads the papers, we have been busy for a number of months in preparing our position so that we can approach the United States in order to discuss and, hopefully, have some action taken in connection with the memorandum of understanding on softwood lumber
entered into in 1986. Conditions since then have changed excessively.
Our position is not made any easier, of course, by the fact that the province of Ontario has never taken any replacement measures in connection with that memorandum of understanding, but rather continues to allow a 15 per cent tax to be imposed in connection with lumber exports from Ontario.
We have met with the Government of Ontario, the Government of British Columbia and other governments and we will be pursuing this matter in the coming months. It may well be, at some time, we will be calling on our Prime Minister who, because of his excellent relationship with the United States, I have no doubt will be very helpful in this matter.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, I do read the newspapers. In the March 4 edition of a national newspaper, the reporter wrote: "Mr. Crosbie is not hopeful he can persuade Washington that changes are needed."
Will the minister finally realize and acknowledge the dramatic extent of the damage done to the softwood lumber industry and when will he finally stand up to the Americans and cancel the agreement?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International TVade):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member has ever thought about this situation: What would our chances be if we had in power today or in the near future, members made up of his own party who have made their career on anti-Americanism and in trying to aggravate and irritate our next door neighbours? Luckily, he has in power a government which has a chance of success in this matter. There would be no chance if his own party was in power.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
One of the many aspects of the recent budget which has not been explained is the legislated limits on government spending of 3 per cent over the next five years.
Presumably this legislation can be repealed at any time during those five years. Can the minister explain what will prevent the government from simply altering its own legislation in the future? What does the government
March 6, 1991

seek by these legislative spending limits that it could not equally achieve by its own budgetary measures?

Mr. Speaker, we have been able to demonstrate, over the past six and a half years, a spending discipline by holding our spending to a rate of growth of 3.7 per cent.
I think it is important for the Canadian people to have confidence that the spending record can continue and that is why we believe it is important to give Canadians that confidence by legislating the spending limits. In that way, they can be assured we can get our deficit down, we can take the pressure off interest rates and we can help the growth in this economy.
My friend asks what is going to stop another government in the future from changing these legislated limits? What will stop governments from changing these legislative limits is if the Canadian people put a priority on maintaining those limits and indicating clearly to their members of Parliament the importance they attach to that because we have seen from the past that excessive spending has resulted in increased taxes. speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me this opportunity to make the comments on not only the budget that was presented last week in this House, but also the expenditures that are before us.
I spent the weekend in the riding of Thunder Bay-Nipigon conversing with many groups concerned about the progress and the direction that this country is facing. Some of the groups that I met with-and they were diverse-were from the ethnic communities, particularly the Lithuanians who were celebrating a particular event of freedom on Sunday. I spoke with some university
Government Orders
students who were concerned about the direction that this country is taking. I also spoke at one of the municipal conferences with a very important segment of our community today, that is, the mayors and reeves representing all of northern Ontario.
I said to those mayors and reeves that they may be the politicians who are most vulnerable in this next period of time. What we are seeing in Canada is a transfer of responsibility for all the obligations that most Canadians have come to expect. We are seeing this government transferring its responsibility from the federal government to the provincial governments and, I am sure, in turn to the reeves and mayors of the municipalities not only in northern Ontario, but throughout this country.
The crux of this is going to be that the municipal politicians, who deserve a great deal of respect for the work they do within their individual communities, are going to be the ones who are faced with the very hard decisions which I suggest this government should have taken. It should have taken the onus of responsibility off those municipal councillors.
What I heard from all of these different sources with respect to how the affairs of this country are being administered was: How can we possibly keep spending more than we take in? Other comments were: How can we run this government by continuing to go into a deficit, into a deficit, into a deficit, without ever having an accounting and without ever having to say to the Canadian people that it is time to catch up?
Other words I heard were: How can we continue to mortgage, not only first mortgage but second and third mortgage, the future of this country to our children and to our grandchildren, when there are absolutely no assets left in this country to mortgage at this time?
The fact of the matter is simply this: since 1984, since this government took office, the debt in this country was $140 billion. That is nothing to be proud of, but it was $140 billion and it was in serviceable and manageable proportions.
We were told and the Canadian people were told that this government which was elected was going to be able to cope not only with the debt, to bring the debt under control and to reduce the debt, but it was going to take into account the annual deficit. At that time it was around $34 billion. It was going to take the annual

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
deficit, reduce it accordingly, and get the financial affairs of this country under some kind of control.
Let us just look and see what happened in the last seven years. The debt is no longer $140 billion, it is now just a little over $400 billion, an increase of $260 billion in seven years. To service that debt in 1984 took about 12 per cent of the federal budget. Now it will be demanding at least 40 per cent of all the money taken in by the federal government.
We were also told in 1984 and again in 1988 that we have to bring our deficit under some kind of control. As we all know, the deficit in those years had been running at approximately $30 billion. What is the budget and what is the deficit that is presented to this House of Commons in the last period?
The deficit has not been reduced one iota. If anything, it has increased, in spite of the fact that this country has experienced seven years of the greatest industrial economic growth that any country in the world has seen. We have increased our taxes at least 17 times. We have almost doubled the amount of revenue brought into the federal treasury and yet we still end up with a deficit of over $30 billion. That is not responsible government and that is not fiscal management.
I am sure that the people of Canada will respond to that at the appropriate time.
Let us talk about some of the details of the budget. The word that I think is so important and the word that really hurts is that the government has brought this country into a recession and the correlative function of a recession, and that is the corresponding unemployment that all Canadians will be experiencing.
This government says freely that it is willing to live with unemployment figures in excess of 10 per cent. This is not acceptable. What it has failed to do, and the operative word which I think is lacking in this budget, is a word that we have heard so much about in the last little while on the international scene and that is linkage. What this government fails to do is link that employment statistic with not how are we going to treat those who are unemployed because of the recession that it has created, but how we are going to correct the problem of unemployment in this country.
The government has failed to link the means to create jobs in this country. I mean simply this. Since 1989, every job that was created in Canada was created by a small business venture. In 1990, that fact presented itself again and, in 1990, every job that was created in this country was created by a small business venture.
What has this government done with respect to small business and the linkage that I talked about? It has not helped small business in this budget. It has done nothing to assist the small businessman so that he could go out in the marketplace and create those jobs that are so vital to the future of this country.
What this government has failed to do is link the problem of unemployment with the problem of how to eliminate that 10 per cent or 11 per cent of unemployment, that linkage that is so necessary. Not only has the government failed to address the linkage, but it has also added to the problem of the small businessman by adding to his expenses, by adding another 24 per cent to his costs of operation, so that it is not only unfair, but it is really and truly an added expense the small businessman can no longer tolerate.
It is unconscionable how the government has avoided the responsibility of helping small business in this country.
I would like to enlarge a bit on larger businesses and some facts which I think are very important and which this government absolutely fails to realize. I hope in every response that I am able to give in this House, I will be able to bring the strongest message I can to the Canadian people and to this government. They are facts which I think we should always bear in mind, and it is perhaps one of Canada's best kept secrets, that forestry is the largest single industry in Canada. It is larger than the automobile and the petroleum sectors combined.
Forestry provides employment to 8 per cent of our Canadian labour force. It supports 900,000 forestry manufacturing and service jobs. One out of every seven manufacturing dollars in Canada is related directly to the forestry industry. It contributes more than $17 billion to Canada's net trade balance, which exceeds that trade balance created by agriculture, fisheries and mining combined.
Forestry accounts for close to $2.5 billion in trade within our country alone. Despite these impressive figures, they do not for one minute reflect what this

government thinks about the forestry industry. It has absolutely forgotten that the forestry industry exists.
Proof of that point is the 15 per cent export tax which is killing, not only the industries I represent, but industries my friends here represent in the softwood lumber industry. It is also starting to have an effect on those industries in British Columbia, in Alberta and our friends in the province of Quebec.
A reduction or elimination of the 15 per cent export tax, if this government was serious about helping Canadians, would not cost the taxpayers of the country one cent to eliminate. The government could eliminate that 15 per cent export tax simply by negotiating its way out of it with our friends in the United States and saying that it is no longer going to be operative.
The memorandum of understanding would be eliminated and section 9 would be invoked 30 days from now. It would give the forestry industry, at least, the opportunity to compete, not only within Canada, but in the United States on an equal playing field so that our forestry, our sawmills and all of those industries that are so important in this country at least have the fair opportunity to compete and be part of this economy.
I appreciate the opportunity of speaking on certain issues that this budget fails to address. I think it is important to address some of the issues that the budget did not address as issues that it did address.

Yes, Sir. Mr. Speaker, I certainly enjoyed listening to my colleague across the aisle as he was telling us his views. Yet I am surprised that he can come up with these figures when you consider the source of this debt we are dealing with today. I must confess I am unhappy about standing up and talking about borrowing money. It is contrary to anything that I believe in and I believe that most Canadians feel that way; that we have to borrow money in order to pay our bills in this country that is so rich in resources, rich in manpower. We have so many things going for us to see the situation that we are in.
Basically what this bill is doing is asking permission to borrow for this year $26.4 billion for the 1991-1992 fiscal year. This amount is equal to the borrowing requirements of $23.4 billion comprised of financial requirements estimated for 1991-1992 of $21.6 billion in

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
exchange fund account earnings of $1.8 billion and a $3 billion non-lapsing reserve to cover contingencies.
This is essentially the same type of thing that we have been borrowing for the last three or four years.
The previous speaker talked about the size of the debt when our government took over. We need to recognize that at the present time 80 per cent of the present debt is due to compounded interest on the debt which we acquired from the previous government.
My comments today are going to be primarily concerned with the government's plan to control that further debt, to control the deficit, and to look at the long-term financial interests of our country.
Since coming to office in 1984 this government has indeed waged a war against the deficit and attempted to restore the health of Canada's finances. Yet, I have not heard at any time any assistance offered by the opposition to cut our spending. Discussion of increasing taxes was immediately said to be wrong, that we could not do it. Any change in our assistance to business such as free trade was decried as something that was disastrous to the country.
I think that this government has been alone in the country in itself in assuming a responsible position. Many people know that last fall I had some problems with my own party and one of the major reasons was that I felt that we were not being tough enough in our financial situation.
When this budget came out I was delighted to see that we were not only dealing with the present situation but also that we were looking forward to the future. I have children, I have grandchildren, and I certainly hope that I will see my great-grandchildren, but I am concerned- and one of the reasons I went into politics was because of the financial situation that our country was facing. The best thing that any government in Canada can do at the present time is stop the debt from dragging down the economy. That means dealing with our annual deficit and getting our spending under control so that we are paying for what we are buying.
Any of our deficit reductions, any of our programs that will balance our budget, will certainly have my support.
I think all Canadians recognize the seriousness of the debt. They recognize that each one of us has to play our own part in solving this problem. It is not something which government can do alone. I think that Canadians want to know that government is doing its part to control expenditures and that each Canadian is getting a fair shake. What the government has done in this budget is to present a program in which everyone is carrying their fair share. In the 1989 budget, I believe the government presented a medium term fiscal plan. What I think we have done this year in the 1990-91 budget is start to look at the long term. I think we are reaffirming the things that we started back in 1984.
If we do have a fault, it is that we did not do more sooner. I would certainly have liked to have seen us take a better grip on that deficit so that our debt today would not be what it is at the present time.
We recognize too at the present time there are people in Canada who are in trouble. We recognize that our western farmers need aid. We recognize also that because of the temporary recession that those who are unemployed need assistance at this time, so the government has seen fit to increase expenditures in these areas of the budget. Also, the disabled are going to receive more benefits. There are going to be tax breaks for employers who make it easier for the disabled to work and to take part in Canadian life.
This country has been living beyond its means for the last two decades. We have been spending more than we have been taking in. In 1984 when this government took over the government was spending $1.33 for every $1 that it was taking in in taxes. In other words, every year we were spending 33 cents more on each $1. We recognize in our own budgets at home that there was no way that this could carry on and we are now reaping the adverse effects of that.
My friends opposite say: "You should have cut the deficit sooner". Yet we recognize that while they were in power that the size of the civil service was growing at 12 to 15 per cent a year. The budgets were growing at the same rate. It takes time to turn that around.
March 6, 1991

We are all aware of a great ocean liner or an air ship that you cannot just all of a sudden reverse these things and expect them to go in the opposite direction. I think that this is also true of government where programs and initiatives have been introduced, that you cannot just abruptly stop them without dislocating the economy. What we have been doing and we will continue to do, and I think at an even greater rate, is to solve these problems to turn the economy around and bring our country back to prosperity.
My friend across the way mentioned that the debt was $400 billion now. The fact is that it is not quite that bad but at some time during the year indeed it is going to reach the level of $400 billion or interpreted in another way, $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The interest alone on this debt, $43 billion, is unavailable for good programs and services in Canada. It is more than we spend on old age security, unemployment insurance and family allowances combined. We recognize what a crippling effect this has on the welfare of our country.
In this budget also the government is asking Canadians to share the burden. We as politicians are being asked. The Prime Minister's budget is being frozen. Cabinet ministers' budgets are being frozen. Senior civil servants are being reduced in number. This is not a particular group of Canadians that is being singled out but indeed all Canadians. As we mentioned earlier, there are exceptions. Those in need, those in times of need have been exempted from this program and we commend the government for that very human attitude.
If the government does not take these steps of fiscal responsibility of limiting expenditures, of limiting transfers to provinces where they can spend federal funds without any responsibility, if we do not do these things then that deficit is going to increase more and more as it has in the past.
We recognize that this government has reduced the deficit by about $10 billion. This year the deficit will be $30.5 billion. They say that this was far above the predictions of finance minister. He could not always predict the problems that western farmers have had, the $2.5 billion which was required to assist them. We just could not see those western farmers left alone. We could not foresee the funds that were required to assist our troops in the Middle East and to assist our allies and to make sure that Canada took its fair share of that
Government Orders
responsibility. Also, the unemployment insurance fund has required more funding than we had expected.
All of these problems have helped to increase that deficit which all of us are sorry about. We recognize that in the next year it will be similar, but after that we will soon start to see the deficit being reduced. This is what we are looking for, so that in the following year the deficit will be down to $25 billion and in 1994-95, in that area, the government will no longer have to bring forward these borrowing bills. We will be able to pay our way and that will be a day of great rejoicing for Canadians everywhere. I am sure they will recognize responsible government when they see it.
One significant thing the government has done is to control the growth in program spending which will be held to an average of no more than 3 per cent annually in the years after 1991-92, owing to an extension of the two-year expenditure control plan.
Also, the government will continue to limit the transfers of payments to provinces, the wealthy provinces, whereas those in need, the poorer provinces, will continue to receive the present amounts.
As I mentioned earlier, after 1993-94, the federal government will be able to stay out of the financial markets. This will allow interest rates in this country to come down. There will be less competition for the funds available and our own companies and industry will be able to borrow at cheaper rates. They will be able to produce more jobs, more manufactured goods, more services to supply Canadians.
I believe that this government does have a very good plan for economic recovery. I think we are going to continue on with that, to control spending that will help put government finances firmly on a course to a balanced budget.
Also in this present 1991 budget, there are certain other things this government has done. For example, it is going to change the way it manages expenditures. Very shortly the government will be releasing legislation which will impose mandatory limits on annual program spending for the next five years.
The other night one of my colleagues asked the question: What type of legislation is this going to be? I told him at that time that I do not know just what that legislation would be, but it will be constitutional because the budget program spending track will indeed be enforced by law. Flexibility will be confined to a very limited set of contingencies set out in the legislation. It

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
will not preclude new programs to meet new needs. In other words, if something comes up unexpectedly, the legislation will certainly allow the government to meet these needs.
The government is going to have to fund these new programs, but within a total legislated budget. In other words, if we acquire a new program, something else will have to be changed or altered to deal with that.
The other nice thing about this budget that I like and has to do with our deficit is the fact that any revenues from the GST above those projected will make a contribution to deficit reduction rather than provide the leeway for an expansion in discretionary government spending. During the GST debate we heard that the GST is nothing but a cash cow and after another election it will be raised 1 or 2 per cent. This legislation is designed to ensure Canadians that any revenue that comes in from the GST is going to go directly to debt reduction.
Many, many people, many businessmen, many senior citizens, many people on the street said to me: "If we were assured, if you could guarantee that the GST will not be used for further programs and frivolous giveaways, then we will accept and we will be happy to contribute to it".
One of the very positive things in this budget is the concept that any proceeds from the GST will be used for this purpose as well as the proceeds from privatization.
We hope that this program continues so that any funding from these sources will also be used to pay the deficit and the debt.
Also, I have been surprised at the number of people who have come forward with individual cheques and cheques from businesses and said: "We want to contribute to the reduction of the debt." So, this is a possibility where citizens themselves can take those funds and help to reduce Canada's debt.
First of all, of course, these funds would be used to service the debt. It would be nice if we could pay off the interest, but that is not the way finances work. We will
service the debt and then as the income grows and as the deficit reduces, we will be able to reduce the debt per se.
In the combination of this program with the proposed annual spending limits, this fund provides assurance that all revenues from the GST will be used to service and reduce the debt and not to fund new program spending. As I say, the people in my riding have said that this is the type of program that they want.
Another factor that was brought out in this budget which shows the clear goal of the government at this time is to set a very realistic limit on inflation.
The Minister of Finance together with the Governor of the Bank of Canada have set the goal of a 2 per cent inflation rate by 1995. This is certainly a very commendable and achievable goal.
In many years during my medical practice, I have lived and worked with older people. Many people had retired with what they thought was a perfectly adequate pension. It was not long before they were finding that they were no longer able to meet their needs.
As a matter of fact, just last night I was talking to a former patient who had phoned. She was concerned about the effects of the GST on her income. She got a rebate of $72 quarterly, so we know what income level she was in. Her furnace had gone on the hummer, and the washing machine and the fridge had problems. She had had to get these repaired, and the GST on top of the service bill was distressing her a great deal.
As we talked, we talked about her municipal taxes. She said that when she moved into the particular home, her taxes were $1,300. At the present time, they were $3,500. We talked about the price of groceries and the price of everything. She began to realize that it was not the GST that was hurting her, but it was the total cost of living.
In other words, the inflation rate, which had been only 4 or 5 per cent in the past, had been increased by the previous administration up to 20 per cent at times. Was it 15 per cent?
Even 5 or 6 per cent for people on fixed incomes is a disaster. I think this goal of the finance minister and the Governor of the Bank of Canada of 2 per cent is highly commendable. It allows businesses and individuals to
March 6, 1991

plan for the future. I think that that is critical in this very unstable world in which we live.
I believe that we, as Canadians, can certainly look forward to that.
This budget is a plan for economic recovery. I believe that the government is taking the action to establish fiscal responsibility and to strengthen confidence in Canada's future. I think that is something which we all need to know.
By reducing the deficit and controlling the public debt, the plan will help to set the stage for improved economic performance and increasing prosperity. It is something that we can pass on to our children in a country in which they can live, grow and prosper.
We can look forward in the hope that within a few years this borrowing authority such as we have to ask for today will no longer be required, or perhaps be substantially smaller than it is in Bill C-79.
I believe that this is just a small indication of the very positive direction being taken by this government and the benefits of the economy in the budget presented on February 26.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the hon. member's debate on the merits of this budget and the merits of this bill, I wondered whether in fact he had listened to all of the other interventions by other members. One of us last night indicated that perhaps what we needed was a shuttle to go back to outer space and bring the finance minister down to earth because the situation is not nearly as he depicts it.
Quite frankly, we have given indications in interventions over the course of the day, and in the course of the debate over the last couple of days, that the circumstances that the Minister of Finance is describing may be true, but it is equally true that over the course of the last six years, under the administration of both that finance minister and that government, what we have had is an increase in personal income taxes to the tune of 9.03 per cent. We have also had a decrease of some 34 per cent in revenues raised from corporations.
No one on this side of the House is suggesting that that was a problem. What is a problem is the fact that the
Government Orders
finance minister is unwilling to acknowledge that perhaps that kind of largess contributed in any way to the competitiveness of our manufacturers, our corporate sector. Clearly, that has not been the case, because our corporate sector, if we take a look at the bankruptcies and the manufacturers that are moving down south as an indication, is clearly not as competitive as we would want it.
What do we have for that 34 per cent reduction in taxes in the corporate sector? What do we have in terms of a government strategy to make our corporations much more competitive? What do we have in return from the government with respect to making our manufacturers much more competitive on the international trade side?
As a bit of a digression, I remind the hon. member that what has happened over the course of the last six years, under the able administration of this government, is that there has been a 60 per cent reduction in balance of payments and international trade. If in fact Canadians have been asked-and they have been asked-and they have been willingly contributing to the government revenues in order to decrease the deficit and the public debt, then we have a right to ask the hon. member and, through him, the finance minister just how they have been managing our moneys.
I remind him that the interest payments on the public debt have increased by only 6.09 per cent over the course of the last six years. That is a grand total, in absolute dollars, of just over $16 billion. But from increased taxation, both from direct and indirect taxes, there has been a net windfall of some $37 billion.
Canadians have a right to ask: What have you done with that money? How can you, with unmitigated gall, come back before this House and ask us once again to contribute more in taxation and to cut back on programs that are vital to the structure of this country all, always, in the name of saying that we must reduce the deficit and the debt? What have you done with the money that you have taken from us in the last six years? And how can you expect us to believe that you are going to do anything worth while with it now?

My mind goes back about six months when I asked the hon. member a question after he had made a similar speech. I asked him to give me a specific way in which his party had helped to reduce the deficit, one measure that they had supported to reduce the deficit, or one tax change which they had supported in any way.
He never did answer the question, in spite of two attempts at pinning him down.
He asked the question about the reduction in corporation taxes. I think if he talks to any of his friends in business, if he talks to any businessmen, he will very quickly learn that businessmen and businesses are paying more taxes than they ever have before. This is one of the real problems that Canadian businesses have, namely, competing with those across the line where they have more beneficial tax structures. Rather than us giving away something and the poor Canadians having to fill in, we hear the opposite side of the story, that by closing the loopholes such as automobiles and cutting down on the luncheon expenses that we heard about earlier, and this type of thing, that indeed these people are spending more and more money in taxes.
If companies are going out of business, it means they are not making any money, and if a business is not profitable it is going to go out, and you cannot tax a company that is going out of business. Therefore, the important thing for Canada is to provide an environment that will encourage business, that will encourage investment, that will encourage the production of jobs which we need.
Somebody said earlier that 90 per cent of the jobs in Canada are from small business. They talk about one or two of the large businesses and the critical thing to me, for Canada's future and prosperity is that small businessman. These are the ones that are going to benefit from the lower interest rates that this budget is going to produce. Canadian business needs to have at the present time the ability to forecast, the ability to predict what next year's needs are going to be, and the ability to have a stable labour force.
It is true that we have increased income taxes, but again, as I say, we had to pay bills, and we still have a deficit in spite of those increased taxes. Therefore, the important thing is to stimulate, to broaden that tax base so that there are more people who are contributing to the economy. Rather than expecting just a few people
and a few businesses to pay the whole shot for the rest of the country, we all have to take our part.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate in this debate on Bill C-97. I also want to express some thoughts and concerns that I have on this government's budget.
I believe that Canadians are increasingly worried about the outlook for their future standard of living. This government's budget has not tackled the problems regarding the finances of this country. The budget is a hollow document. Deficit reduction methods used by the government have been, and continue to be, failures.
The economy is in a recession. The government's deficits and debt levels have ballooned so large that they are growing out of control. The Minister of Finance in this budget, just like his last budget, is continuing on course in passing the buck to the provinces. The federal government has simply transferred the federal fiscal problem to smaller governments. The freeze on the Established Programs Financing will substantially reduced funds available to the provinces and by freezing these transfers to the provinces, the government is most definitely destroying Canada's health care and post-secondary educational systems.
Provinces cannot pay for these without federal support. The cumulative effects of the cuts in the EPF transfers to the provinces is estimated at $28.3 billion by 1995-96. Cutbacks in resources of this magnitude are unprecedented in the history of federal-provincial fiscal relations.
Let me be clear. The loss of federal support to the provinces and the municipalities is going to force them either to increase taxes or cut services. I feel strongly that the credibility of the finance minister's plans to bring the federal finances into a balanced situation, continues to be an annual failure.
I want to speak for a moment in my critic's role. The estimates for the Department of Veterans Affairs start with a 29 per cent increase in departmental administration, an unbelievable $8.94 million. Following this healthy increase in administration come cuts in transfer payments to the veterans affairs programs. Grants to health care treatments and related allowances suffered a 28 per cent reduction and economic support programs

were reduced as well. War veterans allowances and civilian war allowances were reduced by 12 per cent.
We must be aware that a freeze should still allow for the annual inflation rate, but instead specific programs were denied this necessary increase and will suffer. Some of these programs are: assistance in accordance with provisions of the Assist and Fund Regulations, the Army Benevolent Fund, the Royal Canadian Legion, Canadian Veterans Association-United Kingdom, Education Assistance to Children of War Dead, University and Vocational Training, Veterans Insurance, and Management of Property Contracts.
Why do these programs not have the standard 5.6 per cent inflation increase?
While veterans' programs are being cut, the departmental administration is on the defensive. The government, in fact, has effectively declared war on its own employees. It has started the scare tactics of labour unrest as each 1 per cent increase in wage settlements could lead to a loss of 2000 jobs.
The government has forced Prince Edward Islanders and other Canadians to fight to maintain a standard of living during this recession. The effects of contracting out and privatizing have eliminated and continue to eliminate federal government positions in the country.
Allow me to provide a clear picture of what is happening in my constituency. The loss of purchasing power due to wage controls will not only add to the unemployment rate of 16 per cent, but as Public Service employees lose purchasing power to rising inflation, their spending will plunge rapidly and small businesses in my constituency, my community will suffer.
The government has now cut the Canadian Jobs Strategy program. The promise of job retraining no longer exists. In a recent survey, 68 per cent of Prince Edward Islanders said they believe unemployment to be the most pressing problem in that province. Only five per cent say the deficit is the most important and another five per cent say the overall economy is the most serious problem.
Clearly, these statistics speak for themselves-jobs, jobs, jobs.
Government Orders
I strongly feel that this budget will not help our country in any economic way. Between April of 1990 and January of this year Canada lost 288,000 jobs, and since the famous free trade deal, in the manufacturing sector Canadians lost 229,000 jobs, and the unemployment rate keeps climbing.
In terms of trade with the United States: after two years of the free trade deal shipments to Canada are up by three to five per cent while Canadian shipments to the U.S. are only up two per cent. Once again, the scales between Canada and the United States are tipped in the United States' favour.
In terms of bankruptcies for the year 1990: a record total of 11,642 businesses and 42,782 individuals filed for bankruptcy; up 47 per cent from the previous year. In January of this year there were 5,999 businesses in personal bankruptcy, this is up 69 per cent from the same time last year.
In terms of the deficit: in spite of six years of economic growth, which the Minister of Finance himself has called extraordinary, and in spite of 33 separate tax increases, the accumulated public debt has more than doubled from $166 billion in 1984 to $351 billion in 1990, and is expected to climb to $389 billion this year. The people are paying the price.
My colleagues and I constantly talk of the reasons why our country is in a decline. It is declining because this government does not believe in its own people. Government cuts to Established Programs Financing in 1986, 1989 and 1990 will reduce transfer payments to the provinces for education by $8.94 billion between 1986-87 and 1994-95.
Again, the people are paying the price. The promises of training and adjustment to free trade have not yet been put in place. The government has cut all of its $2.8 billion contribution to the unemployment insurance program and has cut back its training programs from $2.2 billion in 1984 to $1.5 billion in 1989. Once again, I say, the people are paying the price.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to my hon. friend opposite as I always do. I wish to raise a question to him regarding veterans, which I know he has a tremendous interest in. He has speculated on the future of veterans affairs. Certainly, he raised the question, in particular,

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
with regards to a decrease in the budget for veterans allowances. He seemed to suggest that this was an inappropriate thing.
It could not help but remind me of the days 35 years ago, during the time of the government of Mr. St. Laurent, when they had horses on the payroll. In this government we do not believe in having horses on the payroll and indeed, we do not believe in having people on the payroll who are not there to receive it.
I think it is obvious, and I am sure my hon. friend would recognize that it is logical, that we should have an annual reduction in its budget simply because a number of those veterans are passing way.
We have in Canada over 600,000 veterans from the three conflicts in which Canada has been involved: World War I and II and Korea. Over 38,000 of those are women. I think the commitment made by the minister the other day when he, if I may quote from page 17914 of Hansard, said at that time:
-I say to all veterans today that your valuable programs are untouched by this budget. Our level of commitment to you is undiminished. My question to the hon. member is: Since he has raised some reservations with respect to the commitment of this government, which I think has been demonstrated to be very positive, I would ask him to bring forth at this time any indication or any evidence he has to suggest that the commitment of this government to our veterans is any less than it should be?

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member opposite for his questions and for his comments. Even though the number of veterans are becoming fewer and fewer I believe, as do many people connected with veterans, that the amount of the pensions, that the amount of money put forth by the government and by governments is never enough. I was assured by the minister the other day that nothing is going to happen to it in the near future. I certainly hope that is the case.
