speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to say a few things about Bill C-97. This bill would enable the government to borrow $26.5 billion. I believe before we allow it to go to the House or take a vote on it, we ought to hear from a number of members around this Chamber about how we feel about the government's budget. I rise in that particular spirit, because I have some fairly strong feelings on the budget of the government this year.
I regret that the gentleman from Delta is not in sight, but I am sure he is within earshot. In responding to my colleague from Eglinton-Lawrence he mentioned that the short answer, in his words, to the question put to him had to do with the legacy of debt, as he characterized it, left by the previous administration.
I am sure that for him, conveniently, that is the short answer. I think he would be the first to agree that it is not the honest answer though, because the honest answer is that the public debt that we are now dealing with is just over twice as much as it was in 1984 when this administration took over.
At some point it seems to me that the government, after six-plus years in office, six and a half years in office, ought to begin taking some responsibility for its mismanagement, for its inaccurate projections, for its wrong guesses.
These are just not words of mine. Let me give you the words of the Minister of Finance, the gentleman who indeed has been the Minister of Finance for this long tiresome, stretch since September, 1984. He has now brought down his seventh budget. Let us have a look at
March 6, 1991

some of his other budgets before we take at face value all the things he tells us with respect to this budget.
For example, in last year's budget, the Minister of Finance forecast that interest rates for last year, 1990, would be 11 per cent. We all know, of course, that he was way off the mark. They were not 11 per cent at all; they were 13 per cent.
Last year, the minister told us that the deficit would fall to $28.5 billion this year. That was his projection just a year ago, that the deficit right now would be $28.5 billion. It is actually $30.5 billion, two billion dollars more.
Let us go back a little further to his second budget, back in 1985. At that time, the minister told us that the deficit for this current year would be $18 billion and, as I just said, of course it is not $18 billion but $30.5 billion. That is a long way off the mark.
You might say that with that kind of lapse in time you can expect some changes. Of course you can. It is not I but the minister who undertook to project in the first place, and he projected five years before the fact what things would be like five years down the road.
We are now down the road that five years, and he is off by a tune of $12.5 billion. That is a fair error. That is a pretty large mistake to make.
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and tell you about some of the other things that he forecast in previous budgets. Last year, for example, he said that personal income taxes would rise by $4.7 billion. Now he tells us they are going to rise by $7.9 billion.
There is an entire litany here of examples where the minister has said one thing by way of forecast and the reality has proven him to be entirely wrong.
If the minister were wrong only in terms of his ability to predict the future, you could not completely hold that against him. You would, I guess, score him for being so foolhardy as to try and make such precise predictions in the first place but, having made them, he ought to be able to stick by them.
That alone is not his cardinal sin, because we all make some errors when it comes to projecting, predicting, calling the shots on times down the road. But where I believe he is really out in left field, where he has done
Government Orders
something that is completely unforgivable, is in the area of making commitments on behalf of the government and then reneging on those commitments. In so far as my own constituency of Burin-St. George's is concerned, with its 158 communities stretched along 1,800 miles of coast line along the south coast of Newfoundland and up around the western comer, the minister will never, I say to him, ever be forgiven for what he and his colleagues did with respect to unemployment insurance; not only the changes, but the wrecking of the whole concept. He will know what I am talking about.
I am referring, in particular, to the commitment undertaken in this House. I challenge anybody opposite to get up and say this commitment was not made. I can point to the pages and the days in Hansard when it was made. It was made over and over again. The commitment to which I refer is the commitment at the time when the government wanted to keep its own troops in line to get Bill C-21, the UI bill, through this House last year. The commitment was made and repeated many times, that the benefactors of this program, the recipients of the UI, would not be asked to bear an unconscionably high increase in rates.
Indeed, there was a commitment made that there would be no appreciable increase in rates over the two or three years. The commitment was also made that in bad economic times the government would kick in. The statement was made again and again, that the fact the government was withdrawing its $2.8 million did not mean the government was out once and for all. In bad economic times, we were told, the government would ante up the difference.
That was the rhetoric last year when they were trying to ram the bill through and when they conned people on the Tory backbench over there into voting for something on the basis of a promise that the government obviously had no intention of keeping, the promise that the government would avoid having UI premiums escalate too quickly, particularly over the next two or three years.
Now we hear the Minister of Finance, less than a year later, say that in conscience they could not allow the fund to be underfunded, so the government had to make this dramatic increase in premiums. I say to the Minister of Finance and his colleagues, that is a classic example of duplicity, a classic example of where the government

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
made a commitment as late as last fall it clearly had no intention of keeping.
When you have in power people who practise that kind of wilful deceit, it is difficult for the electorate to believe a word they say, whether it is about projections of budget deficits or any other matter.
Mr. Speaker, I realize from your signal that my time has just about run out. In specific terms, the government decided to cut $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy program at a time when the fishery is in collapse in much of my riding, both inshore and offshore, and at a time when people were depending on this program to keep the bread and butter on the table, to help them over the short term. For the government to cut $100 million from this program is absolutely and completely callous and unconscionable. I cannot understand where they are coming from in this particular respect.
Let me deal with the area of the Established Programs Financing, the medicare expenditures, the medicare votes to the provinces. I am thinking of my own province of Newfoundland. That is going to cause real problems for Newfoundland. Over the 10-year period since this government first began tampering with Established Programs Financing, and I am talking from about the 1985-1986 budget through until 1995-1996, this government's tampering with medicare will cost the Newfoundland provincial government treasury, $845 million. There will be a shortfall of nearly $1 billion.
It is actually $845 million over that 10-year period which, of course, is going to decrease and constrain considerably the capacity of the Newfoundland government to provide post-secondary schooling and medical care to the half million people who make up my province.
There are so many other things that I would like to say, but I see that my time is up.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened as I always do, with great interest to my hon. friend from Burin-St. George's.
I could not help but be somewhat confused by what seemed to be a somewhat contradictory aspect to his
remarks. He referred to the growth in the public debt in this country during the last six years. I believe what he referred to was the fact that the debt has doubled during the last six years, which indeed is regrettable.
When this government and this Minister of Finance came into office, they inherited a $38 billion deficit, $11 billion of which was on program and operating and $27 billion was on interest charges.
That $11 billion operating deficit has now been turned into-I see in the budget-a $12.7 billion surplus. It is an improvement of $23 billion to $24 billion. My hon. friend says that that is not good enough and that the problem is that the debt has increased.
Mr. Speaker, when you inherit a $38 billion deficit and reduce it to $30.5, that is a tremendous bit of progress. You are still adding $30.5 billion to the debt every year.
The only way that this government could have prevented any growth in the public debt, as my hon. friend seems to suggest it should have done, would have been to wipe out a $38 billion deficit within months of coming into office.
In fact, what the government has done-I think to its credit-is gradually reduce that deficit to the point, as I said before, where an $11 billion operating deficit has become a $12.7 billion operating surplus. My hon. friend says that that is not good enough.
I wonder if he could share with the House how he would have, had he been Minister of Finance in 1984-85, got rid of the $38 billion deficit in one budget.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my friend from South Shore is always a delight to listen to.
In his previous intervention, he reached way back into his bag of tricks to a former Prime Minister, Mr. St. Laurent, and talked about horses being on the bureaucratic payroll.

He says that reducing the debt could not be done. Perhaps he ought not to wait until I am minister of finance. I hope he is better at predicting than his colleague, the present Minister of Finance.
March 6, 1991

Maybe he can do himself the favour of not waiting until I am the minister of finance, but he should get the job himself. He said something a moment ago that is very significant. He told us something that in all fairness he should have told the Minister of Finance five years ago. He tells us it could not be done.
The Minister of Finance did not know that five years ago when he was predicting that it could be done, when he was predicting that it was going to come down to $18 billion. That poor Minister of Finance, with this brain on the backbench, not having the benefit of his knowledge, keeping it to himself, holding the information when the Minister of Finance could have been made to look much more plausible had only the member for South Shore told him what he obviously knew. It could not be done.
Make up your minds, fellows. Is it the Minister of Finance who is right or is it the newly-minted parliamentary secretary. I congratulate him. I knew with all the bellowing he was doing in the House it was a matter of time before it would pay off. I congratulate him on becoming the latest parliamentary secretary.
If he could only become the Minister of Finance and bring the kind of knowledge he just displayed to the front bench. He asks what I would do. I will tell him one thing I would do. I will tell him one thing I would not have done.
I would not have put the public treasury and more to the point, the people of Canada who have mortgages, through those unconscionably high interest rates over the past year or so. Just look at what that has done to keeping up the public debt.
Now, months after we stood here, day in and day out, and argued that high interest rates were not the way to go, lo and behold they have discovered the pages of our book. Listen to the Minister of Finance these days talk about how we have to keep the interest rates down because that is what will cure inflation.
A few months ago the argument was the reverse, we cannot let them come down because that will cause great inflation. Now, fellas, which is it?
What would I do? I would not have allowed John Crow and the crowd over at the Bank of Canada to take over the Government of Canada in terms of fiscal policy and
Government Orders
keep jacking those rates up. They would have come down, our public debt would have been down and our deficit would have been down considerably. That is just one for starters, but there are many others. I would not have had 33 tax increases over the last six years. Does the member want me to go on?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am appreciative of the opportunity to speak on Bill C-97, the borrowing authority legislation. This legislation flows from the budget speech which was delivered last week by the hon. Minister of Finance.
The budget's priority is action to create the essential conditions for recovery. We have chosen not to increase government spending. History shows that that approach has not worked. The key to recovery is lower interest rates. The plan for economic recovery will lead us to lower interest rates through a number of key actions.
First of all, we are setting out clear inflation targets. The result of lower inflation and lower expectations, which is very important, people's expectations of inflation, will result in lower interest rates.

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
Second, we are putting government finances firmly on the course to a balanced budget. We are removing the build-up of public debt as a source of inflationary concern.
The expenditure control plan announced in the 1990 budget is being extended for three years to 1994-95. The government is legislating mandatory program spending limits. We are establishing a Debt Servicing and Reduction Fund solely dedicated to offsetting the costs of public debt. This is something of which I am personally very appreciative.
My constituents, over the past year, have said that they would not mind paying the GST, that they are not adverse to paying taxes if they know the taxes are going to pay the deficit and the debt. People know that we must pay our own way. They know that spending more money than you have coming in creates inflation and inflation hurts everyone. The revenues from the goods and services tax and from privatization will go into this fund.
Third, we are strongly restraining the operations of government. As we all know, government operations are about $16 billion to $16.5 billion, which is about 18 per cent of the program budget. Most of the money that we spend in the Government of Canada is for statutory programs. But, nevertheless, we are severely restraining the operations of government. Operating budgets are being frozen at current levels and the wages and salaries of cabinet ministers, MPs, all Order in Council appointments and all federal public servants are being tightly restrained.
These measures show a fundamental commitment to strong, effective government management and control. This approach will serve Canadians well for years to come.
One other thing we are doing under government operations is moving the National Energy Board to Calgary. This move, I believe, will result in greater efficiencies. Ninety per cent of the business of the National Energy Board is with the oil and gas sector, and its clientele is in Calgary. So, the NEB will be able to interact and regulate the oil and gas industry much more effectively with lower cost to both the people of Canada and to the oil industry. For 15 or 16 years the oil and gas
industry has had to bear the costs of travel and accommodation expenses when they have come to Ottawa in order to do business and to follow the regulations of the National Energy Board.
The Government of Canada will eliminate new federal borrowing in financial markets after 1993-94. I would like to quote from an article written by Jeffrey Simpson last week, entitled "Mr. Wilson chips away at the debt left over from the nightmare years".
Ottawa became a fiscal cripple in the years 1975 to 1984, when the federal government accumulated nearly $200-billion of debt. Compounded interest on that accumulated debt cost another $120-billion by 1989-90. So the total bill for these 10 nightmare years of economic mismanagement, 1975 to 1984, is in the vicinity of $ 320-billion.
This is an impartial commentator, Jeffrey Simpson, from The Globe and Mail. He continues:
It was obvious by the time the Tbries took power in 1984 that, having spent a decade getting into an utterly untenable fiscal situation, Canada would need more than a decade to extricate itself from trouble.
And that is precisely my point. Our borrowing in the financial markets will cease after 1993-94 and by 1995 we will have achieved a balanced budget, roughly ten years after this government assumed office.
He also says in the same article:
Indeed, the entire budget might be described as a treadmill: Higher interest rates make deficit reduction more difficult, large debts make deficit reduction more difficult, recession makes deficit reduction more difficult. Hence, more of the same.
But the fundamental problem remains the size of the debt, close to $400-billion. If the debt were modest in size, say $150-billion, Ottawa's interest payments would be about $16-billion instead of about $42-billion, even at these high rates of interest.
I would like to conclude with this last quote from him:
The cost of paying the interest on this mountain of debt-let alone writing down the principal-would be the grim task of any federal government.
The member from Burin-St. George's decried the fact that we were spending a little less on retraining, and other members have decried the fact that we have been spending less on this program, this program, and this program. Well, the fact remains that even if they were in power-and they will not be because they have flip-flopped on so many issues that Canadians know they are being unrealistic; they know the situation that we are in-they would have to deal with the same sort of debt
March 6, 1991

that we have to deal with. And that necessitates taking hard decisions.
I would like to quote from an editorial in The Globe and Mail of last Saturday, entitled "Ottawa's deficit, in relative terms".
The yardstick by which his progress should be measured is the level
the deficit would have risen to if he had followed the free-spending
ways of his predecessors.
And that is speaking of Michael Wilson.
It goes on to say that:
The Finance Department estimates that, if the parameters of the
1984-85 budget still prevailed -
And I would like to point out that the members opposite would like those parameters to prevail, because they do not want to make any cuts; they do not want to take the hard decisions.
-the deficit would by now be $70-billion a year.
That is double what we now forecast, and $10 billion extra. I shudder to think of such a scenario.
It says that: "Mr. Wilson's current deficit is a considerably tamer beast than the one he inherited". The current deficit is 4.5 per cent of the gross domestic product, the best measure of the total volume of goods and services produced by Canadians.
In 1984-1985 the deficit was 8.7 per cent of the GNP. So, in relative terms of the deficit to the gross domestic product, we have cut that in half. That is a tremendous accomplishment.
It says also: "Nor is the beast as hungry as it once was. In the current fiscal year, Ottawa must turn to the public financial markets for only 15.7 per cent of its cash needs, compared with 27.3 per cent in 1984-1985."
That is a significant accomplishment. Once again, it shows progress. We have almost turned the comer to reducing our deficit markedly. The economy is more productive and in a couple of years our need for cash from the public financial markets will be reduced to zero.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the editorial says; "In real terms, with the effects of inflation factored out, federal program expenditures have shrunk at an average rate of 0.7 per cent during his stewardship. This compares with a real annual growth rate of 5.6 per cent for the previous 15 years-"
Government Orders
This next phrase is significant: "-a period in which the keys to the vault were in the hands of Finance Ministers appointed by Pierre Ihudeau". And the Leader of the Opposition was one of those finance ministers.
Those figures are, of course, with inflation factored out.
That has meant that we have had to restrain expenditures in the program area because the costs of servicing the debt have been growing and have been so enormous. Just think what would happen, how much better off Canadians would be if we had no debt. We would have $16 billion extra a year to make the economy that much more efficient or to provide things like day care or training, or to address some of the structural programs in research and development where an investment might be necessary.
This choice was made by the Liberals in previous years. Because of the debt we have had to use whatever money that has been accrued to the government because of increases in productivity, and so on, we have had to apply that to the deficit and not spend it where it is necessary.
I would like to touch upon the productivity of the Canadian economy. We have seen a lot of productive growth, and this has been very good for us as Canadians. There are three ways in which one can reduce a debt; one is increase taxes, the second is to cut spending; but the third way, and that is the way we have chosen to go in most cases, to increase productivity.
That is what the free trade agreement is all about. That is what the goods and services tax is all about. The goods and services tax will add about $9 billion of productivity to our gross domestic product. That is a lot of income to the government to pay down the debt and in future years perhaps make investments in science and technology and other areas where we deem it necessary.
Our productivity is not as good as it could be. Our productivity performance, the measure of how efficiently we produce and services, has been deteriorating in the manufacturing sector. From 1974 to 1989, over-all productivity growth fell to a quarter of its average level in the previous 20 years. In the first half of the 1980s it did not grow at all. Over the past 15 years, Canada has fallen to fifth from second place among the Group of Seven industrial nations in manufacturing and labour productivity. In fact, over the past six years Canadian manufacturing productivity growth was the poorest among the G-7 countries, despite strong economic growth across

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
other sectors in our industrial economy. Competitors such as West Germany, Italy and France have caught up to and surpassed our productivity levels.
In the 1970s and 1980s Canada's policies were undermining its long-term productivity performance and needed to change course. The 1984 agenda for economic renewal outlined the competitive challenge facing Canada and subsequent actions helped to provide a better framework for restoring productivity growth. Today, as we well know, Canadians are increasingly concerned about their ability to compete. These concerns range from macroeconomic issues, such as inflation, interest rates and the exchange rate to structural problems with our productivity performance, effectiveness of investments, the burden of government and the business climate.
We, as government, have a responsibility to create an environment that encourages the growth of competitive enterprise. The 1991 budget announced actions to restore fiscal balance and to move toward price stability. This will lead to a stable macroeconomic environment, increased confidence in the Canadian economy and will strengthen our ability to compete in a tough economic world.
In working to develop shared approaches to basic economic issues, the federal and provincial ministers of finance are looking at the rising costs of government and at overlap and duplication.
I would like to quote another article from Diane Francis in this week's Maclean's magazine. She states:
Fortunately, Michael Wilson's budget last week continues the Ibries' attack on the debt problem, curtailing program spending to less than the rate of inflation and taking aim at civil-service salaries and transfer payments. The hated GST is a godsend, a money machine whose windfall profits will be legislatively earmarked towards paying the debt. Still, an inability to control interest rates or other government spending plagues Ottawa, with the result that both debts and interest rates are higher than they should be.
It is significant that the provinces in aggregate have a greater share of the economy than the federal government. So what we have done through this budget is we have said we must take a leadership role and we are
encouraging the provinces to restrain their spending to 3 per cent a year.
Diane Francis goes on to say, and this is one of the best descriptions of the debt that I have read:
The debt is frightening. One hour from now, we will all be $3.5 million deeper in debt. By tomorrow, add another $84 million. Ottawa's debt now tallies $388.5 billion, or $15,000 for each man, woman and child, up from $2,591 per head in 1976. This year, it will hit $400 billion. The collective provincial-municipal debt is more than $100 billion, or roughly another $3,850 per person, giving Canadians the dubious distinction of being among the world's most indebted citizens. Hopefully within one year, the deficit, interest rates and unemployment will be much lower, as the recession and the Gulf War end and the GST plus fiscal restraints yield a pay off in the billions.
I am hopeful that that will happen too, that our debt will recede, the recession will lift this summer, and by all means it should, and our policies that we have been putting in place for the last five and six years to make our economy that much more productive will take hold.
It is significant to note that the manufacturing sector shrunk during the 1981-82 recession by 5.5 per cent. During this recession it has shrunk only by about 2.5 per cent. The opposition says all the time: "This factory is shut down due to free trade". These are normal adjustments that happen in every recession and should not be attributed to free trade.
But free trade certainly will help us rationalize our manufacturing and increase our economies of scale and be that much more productive. There will be greater division and specialization of labour, which is very, very important.
So we have been doing the right things. We need to borrow this money to continue on the road which we have set out. We are managing the economy but yet we are looking out for those less fortunate. Most of the increases in this year's program expenditures, 6.9 per cent, which is a high percentage increase in program expenditures, will go to the elderly and to other sectors of society and the economy that need that help, people who have to weather out the recession.
I would like to close by saying that we are doing the right things. We are on a course of recovery. The recession will lift. This budget is a good one. We have learned the lessons from the past, that you cannot spend, spend and spend because that will increase inflation and
March 6, 1991

hurt everyone and drive the economy down to negative economic growth, and that is something we do not want to see.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech of my good friend. He says that his constituents are quite willing to pay taxes as long as they know the money is well used.
To achieve his goals, the minister said the other day that a special fund has been created for the GST. Can my colleague explain in a little more detail just how this fund is going to be administered and what moneys it will contain?

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his question. It is a good one. I, and I am sure he and many other members of the House, will be explaining to Canadians how this fund will work.
The fund will be a separate fund, a national fund, accounting fund to demonstrate to Canadians and to make a commitment to Canadians that revenues from the GST will be put toward the deficit. Revenues from privatization and individual donations that Canadians will make toward debt reduction, will be applied to the deficit.
Also, there is a commitment that this money from the GST is not going to finance more program expenditures which would then necessitate an increase in the GST. People are willing to make the structural change to replace the federal sales tax with the GST because they know it will increase productivity and because they know we are in a terrible deficit situation. They do not want inflation, they do not want negative or low economic growth because of what high deficits and high inflation do.
I remember one of my first town hall meetings after the last budget. A woman came up to me and she presented me with $100 and she said she wanted me to take this to Michael Wilson to apply against the deficit. This is someone that was very, very concerned about the deficit, that was willing to reach into her pocket. This is someone who is a single mother and had a couple of children, divorced from her husband, a teacher struggling to make it on her own; but she was willing to pay $100 toward the debt. I in turn handed that over to the Minister of Finance.
Government Orders
Now there is a place where Canadians can direct any money they want to apply to the deficit, with the assurance that it will go toward paying the deficit.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just a comment here. I heard my colleague say that we have to stop spending, spending, spending. I am quite surprised, because if there is any government that has been spending, spending, spending, it has been this government. I can give him examples of what I call the credibility gap as far as the question of spending is concerned. We can take a look at our beautiful Senate where senators are paid $153 a day just for showing up. It is this government that has actually said: "Go ahead, we will give you the spending"-here is the key word-"increases that you need". It is just probably a paltry sum for the other side; $6 million or $7 million, but for our impoverished senators it is approximately $153 per day when they decide to show up.
It is a coincidence, but I believe I met the same lady in Chambly who met my colleague. She too gave me $100 for my election in order to get this government out of office.
I think it is important that we realize that this government has a credibility gap when it comes to what we would normally call austerity. I remember the night the finance minister was presenting his budget. I walked from the Confederation Building up to the Hill, and I had to weave my way through limousines. We had wall to wall limousines. We still have them, and I do not see any cutbacks at all in the limousine fleet. It is $6 million or $7 million for the Senate and $27 million for the Spicer commission. I know when the Prime Minister is asked, he says $27 million to save Canada is a small sum. Well, I think it is a large sum and I think it is a question of having money well spent. I would certainly welcome an investigation into the Spicer commission.
This is the last point I want to make. This government spent $40 million to make videos of such importance as "Meet your Minister of Defence, Mr. McKnight", which cost $15,000 as well as a video for our troops in Germany on how to drive, another $10,000. This government does not know how to stop spending. This government will only learn how to stop spending when the Canadian public kicks it out of office.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am just sorry that my hon. friend from Chambly was not here to hear me say

that the Minister of Finance increased program expenditures at a rate of .7 per cent during his stewardship. This compares with a rate of 5.6 per cent for the previous 15 years. So we have hardly increased program expenditures.
Yes, you can if you want, pick across the range of $110 billion of expenditures every year. You can pick out little things where we have made mistakes or where we could tighten up expenditures.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the government's request to borrow $26.5 billion and on the budget tabled by the finance minister February 20 this year, and at the same time address some of my personal concerns about the economic future of Canada.
These are not easy times, Mr. Speaker, as you know. In the northwestern parts of Saskatchewan where I come from, the urban and the rural population are feeling the pressures of the recession unlike most in this country.
Throughout the area that I come from, small business people who are still in business tell me that they have never seen things this bad. Consumer spending is way down in all areas. The retail stores, the service sectors and even our small but very important manufacturing sector are all looking for a way out of this economic dilemma.
Our problem in Saskatchewan is the same one that affects the economy in the rest of Canada. It is not a regional problem that requires a regional solution. It is a national problem that only actions by the federal government can correct.
The recession in Canada has been brought on by the high interest rates, the artificially high dollar and high unemployment, each of which exists because of decisions taken by this government under this finance minister.
During this past weekend while I was in my home constituency, I did a lot of thinking about the recession, the local economy and the minister's solution. I also read the newspapers. They provided me with quite a bit of information over the weekend. Perhaps this government has not taken the time to look over some of this important information.
I read The Western Producer among many other farm and rural newspapers. Despite the fact that this government does not understand the value of these farm and rural newspapers and is placing unfair and unreal postal demands on them, these newspapers are going to continue to provide rural people with valuable information. The government would do well to read them regularly.
Last week in the February 28 issue of The Western Producer, we learned that the Saskatchewan and Manitoba economies will fare the worst of all provincial economies in Canada this year.
Quoting from the Conference Board of Canada, The Western Producer said the poorer economies are the result of the general recession and poor grain prices. Again, I remind the government that even with all the diversification in the world, we are still an agricultural economy. To survive, we need improved and stabilized agricultural incomes.
The real decline in provincial output is projected at 0.8 per cent in Manitoba and 0.7 per cent in Saskatchewan. From my reading of the finance minister's budget, there is nothing here that even begins to address the deepening crisis on the prairies. Yes, there is a $1.3 billion tag for agriculture, but as I speak there is still no disclosure of what it is tagged for.
Certainly, the government spending estimates tabled Thursday did not give us any idea of the new priorities and neither did the agricultural ministers' announcement Saturday, following their meeting in Saskatchewan. In fact, the more we examine the announcements, it seems that the federal government's so-called new money is tied up in the GRIP and NISA programs, neither of which is expected to have any impact on the early part of this year's farm income picture.
March 6, 1991

My remarks on GRIP and NISA will have to wait for another day when the enabling legislation is reviewed and debated in this House.
Let me say this, my biggest criticism to date is that the federal government, with the help of Saskatchewan Premier Grant Devine, is selling GRIP and NISA throughout the west aggressively but without detail, without agreement and without legislative approval.
Before the legislation was introduced earlier this week providing the federal government authority to enter into negotiations with the provinces, the Saskatchewan government had already held some 40 information meetings across the province to discuss a package that they had not even agreed upon.
There is not a farmer in Saskatchewan as I speak who can tell you what GRIP will cost him or her in the coming year. Therefore, I ask: How can the farm person properly assess the short and long term effects of this very important program?
On top of this, Premier Grant Devine was quoted in Monday's Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. He was trying to blackmail farmers into signing up for the program. The lead in that Star-Phoenix newspaper story reads: "If farmers expect Ottawa to help them out this spring they'd better sign up for GRIP, says Premier Grant Devine." The is the lead of the story on the front page of Monday's Saskatoon Star-Phoenix.
Here we are trying to assess whether a very important and expensive federal government agriculture and economic initiative is as good as we are being told it is, and the two levels of government are forcing farmers to buy into it without details being announced and even before the legislation is introduced into this Chamber.
We cannot help but be sceptical in all of this. The snow is starting to melt on the prairies and in the near future the crops will be seeded for another year. The farm community has been let down by these governments, many times in the recent past by this government, and now with a Saskatchewan provincial election imminent the farm community is very much concerned.
Remember last year, Mr. Speaker, this federal government told Canadian farmers that they did not need the interest-free cash advance any longer. The government did their studies and they provided evidence to this
Government Orders
Chamber to prove that the interest-free cash advance program should go. Amid sound and reasoned articulate arguments to the contrary from this side of the House and from agricultural organizations the government decided to pass the legislation in any case, and they did away with the program.
Only they were wrong. The program was needed. It was essential and the government had to reinstate it later this fall. Low prices, low sales, and congested elevators, all those things that existed when the program was created in the first place forced the reinstatement of the program. There was a need.
It was not that long ago that the Western Grain Stabilization Program was tampered with by this government. Announcements were made about big pay-outs, and then there were premium increases foist upon the farmers, and the cheques went out and the farmers paid their bills, only to find out that Ottawa had overpaid the producers and that Ottawa was sending out bills of their own for collection on the overpayments. When it was all over the farmers who thought they were getting a stabilization payment and used it to pay their bills found themselves owing even more money to the federal government.
The new agriculture programs GRIP and NISA may indeed help the producer, but we should not as a nation be committing ourselves to it until we understand it in all its parts. The programs are too important not to be reviewed and all their faults debated, reviewed, and corrected without pressure or deadlines.
If a long-term program cannot be agreed upon shortterm financing and debt moratoria can bridge the gap until agreements can be reached on a proper and adequate program.
As for this years bridge, the finance minister's budget does not tell us anything, but we as prairie representatives want him to know and understand that we need almost all of that budgeted $1.3 billion for spring seeding this year, regardless of what happens to GRIP and NISA in the future.
Farm organizations such as the prairie pools and the National Farmers' Union are asking that the seeding payment be the equivalent of the loss in net income sustained by grains and oilseed farmers in 1990. This should mean by itself a payment in excess of $1 billion. A substantial program is necessary to carry farm financing

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
through until the much-needed farm safety net program is in place.
The farm population has come through nearly seven years of inadequate grain prices and have had to battle other rising costs, high interest rates, and decreasing government support.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is clear that the national debt and the deficit are central to the debate on borrowing authority legislation. It is equally clear that as a government, we cannot afford to simply spend our way out of the current recession. This simple solution, recommended by followers of Keynesian economics, simply will not work when we have already had 20 consecutive years of deficits. It would be tantamount to piling debt on top of debt, and frankly, Mr. Speaker, we have had enough. We cannot continue on this path of progressive indebtedness because it is literally the road to ruin.
The Budget tabled by my colleague, the hon. Michael Wilson, opts for another route that leads to economic recovery and prosperity, thanks to measures designed to lower interest rates. At the same time, however, we must substantially reduce federal borrowing and spending if the drop in interest rates is to be more than just passing phase.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should recall at this point that the consultations that preceded the drafting of this Budget included business groups, labour unions and other groups. Generally, they strongly recommended taking steps to lower interest rates in order to stimulate the economy and help the government improve its financial situation. That is exactly what we are doing now.

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
Interest rates and deficits are directly related to that metaphorical ball and chain we call the national debt. Consider, if you will, the national debt, Mr. Speaker.
By the summer of 1991, our national debt will be $400 billion. Some people will say: What is a billion? Let me give you a simple example to illustrate what one billion means. If a person had put $1,000 a day in a plate, every day of every year, starting with the year one of our present calendar, by December 31, 1991, that person would have accumulated less than three quarters of one billion dollars. That same person would have to keep setting aside $1,000 a day, every year, for another 746 years, in other words, until the end of 2739, before reaching the one billion mark. As they say in French, a billion is not exactly a small beer. Our anglophone colleagues would say: It's certainly ain't peanuts.
This year, the national debt works out to the equivalent of a personal debt of $15,000 for each man, woman and child living in Canada.
Just imagine, every time a baby is bom is this country, it is saddled with a debt of $15,000. Assuming that interest rates remain at a steady level of 12 per cent annually, this means that when that baby is six, his debt will have increased to $30,000 and by the time he is twelve it will be $60,000. When as a student, he finishes high school, he will have a debt of $120,000 without ever having borrowed a cent.

That is the happy result of compound interest on the lending side, but it is the sad and brutal reality of compound interest if you must borrow money. It helps explain why our national debt, which was at the $200 billion level when our government took office in 1984, will reach double that figure this year.
More than 80 per cent of that increase can be attached to the compounding interest on the original $200 billion. It is also the main reason why the annual deficit is still at $30 billion in spite of the reduction in spending, and the increased revenue actions taken over the past six years. The interest costs alone on the accumulated debt this coming fiscal year will be $43 billion. That is $1,650 out of the pockets and purses of every Canadian.
It means there is that much less money available for medicare, research and development, job creation and many other programs that would be so helpful to
Canadians. We must get off the treadmill of debt. That means reducing the burden of rapidly growing interest payments.
To do this we must deal firmly with the greatest single threat to economic progress: high inflation. Lowering inflation enables interest rates to come down. Low interest rates allow existing businesses and new businesses to create more jobs, help our country to be more competitive, and contribute to increase our over-all prosperity.
That is the path chosen in the budget for bringing about a recovery of the economy, a recovery that will be sustainable over the long term.

Lower inflation, lower interest rates and lower annual deficits are each others complement and are all factors that tend to stimulate strong economic recovery.
Ever since we inherited this unyielding deficit in 1984, our government has made an incredible effort to reduce operating expenditures.
Spending on all government programs and services has been maintained at levels well below the growth rate of the economy and the rate of inflation.
We have reduced operating costs of government services despite an increased workload. The number of public servants has been reduced considerably. Budgets for travel by elected representatives and public servants have been cut. A number of government agencies have been wound up, and we have privatized several Crown corporations.
In the years to come we intend to continue our unceasing struggle against inefficiency and irresponsible spending.
When we took over the government of this country, the previous federal government was spending $16 billion more on operating expenditures than it received in revenue. As a result, we had to collect $130 in taxes to provide $100 worth of government services, and Canada had an operating deficit.
At the end of the last financial year, this operating deficit had turned into a $9 billion surplus. This means that during the first five years the Progressive Conservative government was in power, we managed to bring about a complete reversal of this situation to the tune $25 billion. Our government has engineered a basic
March 6, 1991

structural change by restoring a stabler balance between expenditures and revenues.
Mr. Speaker, the debt load will become lighter as the national debt takes less and less government revenues. But despite the positive measures that have been adopted we must admit that our priority objective-reducing the debt-remains beyond range unless we impose further restraints. The 1970s and early 1980s were highlighted by a carefree approach based on precarious abundance. This and the next decade will bring us back to stark reality.
If the servicing of the national debt continues to take an ever larger portion of the government expenditure budget, there will of course be less and less money available to maintain the programs which Canadians want because soon they will no longer be able to afford them.
Mr. Speaker, time has come for each of us to assume our collective responsibilities. There can be no reduction in our annual deficit and in our national debt unless we have a flourishing economy. Prosperity can only flown from lower interest and inflation rates. The best way to achieve this goal is to draw inspiration from the example of a government like ours which controls its own operating expenditures. Since a significant part of government outlays is accounted for by public service wages, we have decided to set strict limits on wage increases.
Mr. Speaker, hon. members should note that, generally speaking since 1984, federal government wage increases have been under the inflation rate and less generous than in the private sector.
The budget tabled recently by my colleague Michael Wilson re-affirms our government commitment to continue along that line by indicating just where the line has to be drawn.
As a result there will be no increase in the salary budgets of the departments for the next fiscal year, and raises will be limited to 3 per cent the two years after that. In addition the number of senior officials in the Public Service will be reduced by 10 per cent.
As hon. members already know, Mr. Speaker, the rate of salary increases for the Prime Minister, Cabinet ministers and all MPs has also been limited one way or another.
Government Orders
We are going to innovate by adopting legislation to limit the annual growth of government expenditures at 3 per cent beginning with the fiscal year 1991-92 until the end of 1995-96. This legislation will also indicate that any new spending program will have to be funded by reducing appropriations for existing programs.
The second major budget innovation is the creation of a special debt reduction fund made up of net GST revenues and monies from the privatization of Crown corporations.
In the budget the government indicates that it will cut the annual deficit down to $6.5 billion by the end of 1996 and do away altogether with the need to borrow on the financial markets by 1994.
Thanks to this so ably targeted action plan we can expect that, by 1995-96, the deficit will be down to less than 1 per cent of the gross national product compared to 4 per cent in 1990 and 9 per cent in 1984 when we inherited the disastrous results of the extravagances of the previous government members who seemed bent on spending as if money was going out of style.
When I talk about targeted action, Mr. Speaker, I am referring of course to the agreement between our Minister of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada to bring the inflation rate down to 3 per cent by the end of 1992 and 2 per cent by 1995.

Let me remind all hon. members why we are taking these strong restraint measures. We are acting now in order to secure a better, more prosperous future. The key to improved living standards is continued increases in productivity. By restraining and reducing government's demand for borrowing, we can bring down interest rates and inflation. Lower interest rates encourage investment which in turn, will enhance our national productivity.
I want to comment on what my hon. colleague, the Minister of Finance, has called "the prosperity challenge". Countries all over the world, and Canada is no exception, are being forced to face up to rapid changes in the global economy, largely brought about by technological change. No country can afford to isolate itself from the global marketplace which is developing so quickly. To cut oneself off would clearly bring a terrible drop in a nation's standard of living. But to participate in the global market successfully, requires that a nation's

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
economy must be as productive and as effective as the best in the world.
For Canada, as for all countries, this means making many changes and adjustments so that we get the most out of our national assets and advantages. And the Canadian labour force is, I believe, the most important among all our national resources.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from Chapter 7 of the budget document tabled in the House last Tbesday. It is entitled "Securing Canada's Prosperity: Building an Agenda for Long-term Growth in Living Standards". Under the heading "Better labour-management interaction" we can read this: "Even with the best technology and workforce skills in the world, our productivity performance would still depend fundamentally on how these are integrated in the work place. And that depends on management and workers".
Mr. Speaker, this essential fact must be appreciated at its real value. It stands to reason that we cannot achieve increased prosperity for every Canadian man and woman simply by implementing macro-economic policies designed to control inflation and keep interest rates down. We must also be concerned about the way we can work in association with others and the way we consult one another with respect to the definition of our economic goals.
Unfortunately the way human beings behave in their relations with others does not change as quickly as technology. In fact the attitudes, the human perceptions and the ways to communicate are probably the most difficult aspects to change for any one individual. Yet the significance and nature of these changes are vital.
As I see it, Mr. Speaker, the fact that we can work efficiently together and especially the fact that private sector workers and employers do manage to co-operate in harmony is the most essential aspect of our quest for future prosperity.
As a government our first task is to convince all Canadians that it has become imperative to control the deficit and to prove to them that all our energies and all our decisions will be aimed at that goal. I may have said
this before, Mr. Speaker, but I want to emphasize the fact that this government must take whatever radical measures are required to lower interest rates, inflation and the national debt.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I invite all Canadians to read the guidelines of this historical Budget, that marks the beginning of a new era for us, our children, and our grand-children, because, first of all, as we have shown since we were first elected in 1984, we have never sheened our responsibilities, knowing full well that in the immediate future some of our decisions would not be very popular.
Secondly, the Expenditure Control Plan included in the Budget, and which freezes at current levels the wages and salaries of the Prime Minister, Members of Parliament, senior executives and all federal public servants, as well as the operating budgets, is an example all public and private executives throughout Canada should follow.
Thirdly, all the hard work our government has been doing to get rid of the annual operating deficit and reduce the national debt will generate the lower interest rate and inflation rate essential to our economic recovery and general prosperity.
Fourthly, greater harmony between employees and employers is essential if we are to increase our labour productivity, which will give everyone the opportunity to benefit from our renewed prosperity.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, this Budget marks out very carefully the way for our economic future. It clearly indicates what traps to avoid and what goals to achieve.
We are on the right track, and all Canadians will benefit from this new Budget.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this budget and the estimates. I wish the Minister of Finance had presented last week a somewhat less stringent budget, especially in this time of recession. I suggest the moment was not right to present such a budget, the more so because Canada had experienced a very high rate of economic growth over the past five or six years. We could have then expected the Minister of Finance to present such a budget, but certainly not now.
In view of this high rate of economic growth and also the 33 tax increases, we must wonder where those dollars went? This recession which is due to the government's high interest rate policy is really hurting Canadians. I need only mention the number of bankruptcies which reached 54,000 last year, compared with 34,000 in 1982.
Let us talk also about unemployment. According to the Minister of Finance unemployment will reach 10 per cent in 1991 and 9.8 per cent in 1992.
Does this mean it will take another 18 months to get out of this terrible recession? We hope not.
Before he brought down his Budget, the Minister of Finance implied it would contain measures to help small businesses. We saw nothing of the kind in the Budget. I hoped to see the flow-through shares program renewed, since mining operations are down to 15 per cent of what they were five years ago. Just think, Mr. Speaker: It takes about eight years to develop a mine, from the day it is discovered to the day it becomes operational. Needless to say, in Northern Ontario we are very concerned about what will happen during the next 10 or 20 years.
Mr. Speaker, I also noticed that the Minister of Finance did not raise taxes for corporations, big companies and individuals with high salaries. When this government came to power, corporate taxes were at 13.5 per cent, while today, they are down to 9 per cent, which does not make sense, Mr. Speaker.
And let's talk for awhile about transfer payments to the provinces. During the next few years, we will be seeing cutbacks totalling $2.3 billion in transfer payments to the provinces, which will cause quite a stir in health care and education across Canada.
If people expect to get the same services they had before, they can also expect tax increases, both provincial and municipal. This means that the government has abdicated its responsibility, and that in the final instance, the taxpayer pays just the same.
I mentioned unemployment earlier. Unemployment insurance premiums will go up by 24 per cent next year, which means an additional $2.4 billion in revenue. At the same time, the Minister of Finance has cut $100 million in the budget for occupational training. I find it hard to see the logic in all this.
Occupational training is very important for Northern Ontario, because during the past 10 or 15 years, our young people have been leaving Northern Ontario in a steady stream towards the south, due to a lack of jobs. And what about our unemployed worker, 13 or 14 per cent, who would have liked to train for another job or go back to school or simply upgrade their skills. This $100 million cutback will affect us quite severely, and we find this extremely hard to take.
As far as housing is concerned, the government also intends to cut $35 million in programs for people on low incomes or people living very close to the poverty line. This cutback affects the neediest in our society, and I find it incredible that in a country as rich as Canada, there are still people who have to live in cabins without plumbing, and because of these cutbacks, when people ask for government assistance, they won't get it.

There is nothing in this budget to remedy the awful economic situation in northern Ontario. There are two main culprits: First, the export surtax on softwood lumber is killing the sawmill industry very dramatically. Second, mining exploration is down to 15 per cent in comparison to what it was five years ago. One only has to
March 6, 1991

remember that it takes eight years to develop a mine, from the day of its discovery to its first day of exploitation. Northern Ontarians do have reasons to be afraid for the future.
There is no program either for the industrial development of the infrastructure in order to attract businesses to northern Ontario.
To conclude, I could not finish my remarks without making reference to the natives who have to live in despicable living conditions. Housing is badly needed, and even then there are budget cuts. In some First Nation communities I have seen houses where there are 17 persons living there. In view of the fact that Indian self-government is in the works, there is nothing in this budget to spur economic development on reserves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada is now in a recession. Although there are already indications that the recession is going to be deeper than was expected initially, all Canadians hope that this recession is indeed short.
Periods of recession should be the time to increase spending, in order to help those who are unemployed and suffering hardships, as well as to prepare the country for recovery. However, because of the lack of progress which the government has made in its seven years in office, there is very little room to manoeuvre without doing more harm to the economy.
It is, however, extremely unwise to consider the two events, that is, first the recession, and second our fiscal difficulties to be wholly unrelated. In my last year's budget critique, it will be remembered that I questioned the wisdom of using interest rates and monetary policy to combat inflation without co-ordinating them with fiscal policy.
I have repeatedly asked the finance minister to present information on the inflationary impact of his budget policies. The finance minister's failure to ensure that the government's fiscal policies are co-ordinated with its monetary policies, is incompetent at best.
The facts are evident, as I predicted last year. The use of monetary policy on its own was the equivalent of throwing water on the entire country to put out a fire, a fire which in part the government was itself stoking. In
Government Orders
fact, the finance minister finally acknowledged this fact just this past weekend, saying that his tax reform proposals, while intended to make voters happy before an election, also fuelled inflation.
This year's budget attempts to lay the blame for the recession on inflation. However, inflation is not the big problem, which the government keeps saying it is. The big problem, as I stated last year, is that it is economically dangerous to deal with Canada's fiscal, monetary, interest rate, dollar trade and social policies as though they could be looked upon as mutually exclusive.
All of Canada's policies must be co-ordinated, to ensure that there is a coherent plan and that all government policies are working toward the same goal of strengthening Canada's economy.
During this government's term there have been changes to help ensure that Canada has the required economic vitality to enter the 21st century. At the same time, the government's policies of high levels of taxation, spending and borrowing, and the failure to deal with the long-run effects of borrowing approximately $30 billion annually, have affected domestic interest rates and the value of the Canadian dollar. These policies are working in fact at cross-purposes to our trade policies.
It is unfortunate that Canadians are seeing the negative and damaging effects of thinking that the government has a free trade policy, a social safety net policy, a fiscal and a monetary policy and that somehow each of these can be thought of and dealt with independently. The fact is that these policies are inter-related and trying to deal with them independently has helped to produce what has been called the first made-in-Canada recession.
The failure to get our fiscal house in order is seriously putting our economic strength, our international competitiveness, and even Canada's cherished social safety net programs at risk. Certainly a prime example of the lack of integration in government policy can be seen in its UI reforms under Bill C-21. We see that premiums are up 24.4 per cent this year to fund the increased payouts due to the recession. The increase in taxation will no doubt further hurt the competitiveness of employers whose cash flow and profitability are already hurt by the recession.

Government Orders
Of course the bottom line in this budget, even as we hear about the great cuts, even with $7 billion worth of additional revenues and $1.1 billion worth of cuts, the government is just managing to keep the lid on the deficit. Certainly the government has made steps in reducing the deficit. However, these steps needed to be taken much earlier.
I see, in fact, some of the initiatives announced in the budget are mirrored in Reform Party policy and my own statements. But even a mirror is only a reflection and certainly not the real thing.
For instance, I am glad to see the government has indicated its willingness to create a debt servicing and debt reduction fund, and also set legislative spending limits on itself. Several months ago I asked the government to set up a deficit and debt retirement fund when I announced my pay cut in September 1990.
These proposals are good initial steps to address the wish of the tax paying public that their tax dollars will be used to reduce the deficit and not to pay for new government programs prior to the next election.
However, now that the government has indicated its willingness to take these initial steps, I challenge the government to demonstrate its own sincere commitment by amending the Auditor General Act to require him to report on the impact of all new spending, including the incremental interest costs on the deficit. This will help to demonstrate that the government is willing to abide by its own spending commitments and not produce any new commitments.
The temptation to use any excess revenues for a good news agenda may well be tempting. I know already from my constituents that the remittances of the GST are improving the government's cash flow at the taxpayers' expense. Let that be enough of a benefit for the government.
Canada cannot afford another spending spree before the next election. Last year the finance minister predicted a $26.8 billion deficit for fiscal 1992. In 1989 the minister predicted a deficit of some $23 billion for this year, and in 1984, his first budget while in office, he predicted a deficit of approximately $10 billion by fiscal 1992. So we have a difference, a mistake or a discrepancy of $20 billion, and the debt is many billions of dollars higher than that.
I believe it to be self-evident that the government has for too long deviated from its course and should not again forget its way.
As I have said previously, the government should begin cutting at the top. However, a one year freeze in cabinet salaries and a cap on the growth in MPs' and senators' salaries is hardly a start or a major sacrifice, indeed not even a symbol.
Previously, I have called for cuts to the public service, in particular to the thick layers of middle management. When the Reform Party of Canada suggested a 10 to 15 per cent cut in this area, the government said it could not be done. The government had "cut to the bone already", it said. But now it is possible to cut 10 per cent in this budget. People would ask why.
Because, as with each time the government cuts- whether it is to sell the GST at seven per cent in December 1989, find $350 million to fight the war in the gulf in the fall of 1990, or now in the winter of 1991 to try to regain its supporters and credibility at home and abroad-it is not to reduce unnecessary and wasteful spending, but rather to meet the current crisis facing the country and the government.
That is the key to understanding this government's record on deficit reduction. Unfortunately, it has much more to do with crisis than with commitment.
I want to point out that a dollar that could have been cut in 1984, but which the government did not feel compelled to cut back then, has added approximately $10.40 to our national debt. That is $7 in principal and $3.40 in interest. That is the result of not taking the deficit and unnecessary spending seriously and the effect of not acting sooner. This fact, no doubt, inspired the Prime Minister to admit recently before a group of students, and I quote:
I do not want to suggest we could not have done more, because we
could have done more-Had we done more earlier, our problems
would be less, there is no doubt about it.
Commitment would have reduced the deficit in 1984; crisis reduces it now. Why has it taken seven years for government backbenchers to demand that their government cut wasteful spending?
Finally, I have concerns about the government further cutting conditional transfers to the provinces. The government maintains its own pet programs instead of cutting them and saving money, while it passes taxation on to the provinces. But, by cutting back funding to the provinces while indicating that the federal government will not only continue, but increase legislating in areas of
March 6, 1991

provincial jurisdiction, the government is heading toward a constitutional crisis which clearly neither the government nor the country can afford.
The government may claim that its current unpopularity is the result of making tough decisions. I claim, however, that for the most part the government has not planned these tough decisions, but rather they were thrust upon them by economic events dictating change, the result of having no long-term economic plan for Canada beyond the last election.
A journalist asked me recently how I would rate this budget on a scale of one to ten. I thought for a moment and said that I would give it a five. My snap judgement appeared to be right.
This budget is average. But unfortunately, an average budget is exactly what the government has given Canada for far too long.
For this reason, this budget critique is a eulogy for a government which has waited too long and only done the bare minimum in once again just holding the line. It has done that for seven years; held the line at about a $30 billion deficit. This was hardly enough, and we see the consequences of it now. The country and the government have only to ask what went wrong for seven years. Perhaps five years ago it would have been a good budget, but not now.
Unfortunately, it is too little because it is too late.
In conclusion, this is a budget which tries to win back to a government its supporters in the domestic and international communities and to raise its sagging popularity with the Canadian people. Canadians are looking at it and feeling a great sense of remorse and a feeling of eulogizing for this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to comment on the government's recent economic initiatives. The budget of the finance minister is an incredible disappointment to all those in Canada who had hoped that he would deal with the real substance of the issue of Canadian competitiveness.
The minister has at last acknowledged that the deficit is a problem, and it is indeed when our national debt exceeds $400 billion. But what has he offered us? He has offered us simply the promise that in the future he will
Government Orders
be able to deal with it. But Canadians realize that we are not going to be able to tax our way out of the deficit; we are already overtaxed. And we are not going to be able simply to cut our way out of the deficit. The government has already slashed all sorts of programs and we have seen that it has had no impact on the deficit. It is still far above levels that he predicted years ago, levels he predicted even one year ago.
We cannot tax our way out of the deficit. We cannot cut our way out of the deficit. There is only one solution: we have to earn our way out.
The problem we face is that in his last budget the minister has denied to Canadian industry some of the tools that they used to have in terms of dealing with competitiveness. This is a government that has cut transfers for educational training, has put a cap on funding for export development and promotion, and has put a cap on science and technology. This government is denying to our industries some of the tools which they need to be competitive. As a result, in the last two years, the two years since free trade, Canada has lost 229,000, or fully 11 per cent, of all of our manufacturing jobs. This is a government that is presiding over the deindustrialization of Canada.
At the heart of this problem is a government which is not prepared to assume its proper role in the wealth creation process in Canada. At the heart of our economic dilemma we find a paradox, the paradox being a government that is not prepared to act like a government. It is a government that refuses to play the role that only governments can play, and which is played by every one of our major competitors, in terms of helping industries and working with industries to make them globally competitive.
I am not calling for a government imposed strategy. Rather, what is critical is that the government assume its proper role and bring to the wealth creation process the tools which only governments can bring.
It is easy to criticize this government for its record on many accounts, but I leave that up to others today. Rather, I seek to suggest to this House that there are positive ways in which we can proceed to get around the problem of competitiveness, a problem of declining competitiveness, which our finance minister has recognized but which he has refused to deal with in any

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
fundamental way. Let me suggest what some of these routes might be.
First, we need an entirely new spirit of co-operation in Canada. It is a long time gone. When we could have management fighting labour, fighting educators, fighting financiers, we are going to need the co-operation of all sectors of our economy working in harmony and working in harmony toward common goals.
Second, and I know this is going to sound anathema to some of my Conservative colleagues in this House, we are going to have to plan for our economic future.
Government must be able to bring the key players to the table to discuss what our future can be in five, ten and twenty-five years down the road and to plan for that future. If we do not plan for it, surely it is the ultimate naivety and surely it will not come about. Our competitors plan and even businesses plan for their long-term futures.
Third, I suggest that we cannot be the best at everything in the world because no nation is. We are going to have to build on the strengths that we have already in Canada. I suggest this involves industry such as transportation, communications, and a number of others which we all know, making abundant use of our primary resources, because it is such a squandering of our given wealth to sell those goods away to other countries without adding value to them here in Canada and creating the jobs here rather than having the jobs exported to other nations.
We are going to have to look at some of the industries of the future: biotechnology, specialty metals, many of these.
Fourth, we are going to have to concentrate on our human resources. We cannot have a strong economic future without having the best trained and best educated people. We need more scientists, more engineers, and fewer lawyers.
Fifth is research and development, science and technology. Under this government, R and D spending has fallen from 1.42 per cent to 1.28 per cent of our GDP. It is going in the wrong direction. This can be reversed. Why did they cap science and technology spending in this budget?
Sixth is foreign control. As long as more and more of our Canadian industries fall into foreign hands, we are not going to enjoy the benefits in Canada or the repatriation of profits of the R and D being done here, of the best jobs being in Canada. Besides, we are losing control over our own economic destiny.
Seventh is the monetary policy. Surely we cannot trust a finance minister who has promised us for many years that he will get interest rates down, that he will curb inflation, that he will get the deficit down, and rely on those promises that he is going to do it in the future. He has destroyed all his credibility. I hope he can do it, but for this year alone in his budget he has promised us interest rates just slightly below what they are today, 9.5 per cent. The Americans, against whom we are competing, have interest rates which are almost four points lower than Canada. We have got to get our dollar down to a level that reflects our labour productivity in manufacturing.
Eighth, in terms of infrastructure, for over a century and a quarter that Canada has benefited from its unique mix of public sector-private sector involvement in our economy. The building of canals, of railroads, of the Trans-Canada Highway, of the CBC, of national airlines and of aerospace industries has not come about by market forces or chance.
In summary, whether we like it or not, our competitiveness and our ability to create wealth in the future is dependent upon a government with a philosophy which says that we have a critical role to play in the wealth creation process in Canada.
We have a key role, the role of bringing the players together, of helping set plans, of producing the infrastructure, the educated, trained people, the research and development, the science and technology culture.
I am afraid that if the government does not learn to assume its proper role in the economy of the future that economy will not be ours.
As more and more jobs leave Canada and move south of the border so do the hopes of a whole generation of young Canadians. The bright light at the end of the tunnel is that there is another and better way to deal with our economic challenges but it requires a government prepared to assume its proper role.

March 6, 1991
