speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do appreciate this opportunity to participate in this debate and I do have to commend the hon. member for Willowdale for what I think are some very appropriate comments. Maybe later on in my speech I will try to respond to some of those because I think he made some very valuable suggestions that maybe I can respond to in due course.
But before I do I would like to make some other comments on this borrowing bill, the fact that we need to borrow money, and I think the place to start is probably by an article that I read in The Globe and Mail on February 28. It relates to a speech that the premier of New Brunswick gave while he was in Toronto on a government mission. I would like to quote a paragraph from it: "Governments must conduct themselves like private citizens, borrow if necessary for capital assets such as a new home, but pay as you go for current expenditures like the groceries".
That was from Premier McKenna of New Brunswick. Further on in the article he went on to say: "The leaders of the 1960s and 1970s have placed a first mortgage on the future of Canada. The leaders of the 1980s and 1990s are placing a second mortgage on the same asset. There is no equity left. We must once and for all put an end to the suffocating debt load we are placing on the backs of our children".
Very interesting comments from a Liberal premier in this country because it certainly reflects a different view than we have heard in this House during the debates that we are presently involved in dealing with this budget and the borrowing requirements that emanate from it.
The reason I am pleased to participate in this debate is because of the very clear things that the Government of Canada is doing in trying to deal with the problems of debt and the circumstances that come from it.
I would like to explain why. I happen to represent the riding of Ontario. In my constituency, as I am sure happens in many other parts of Canada, the question is "what are we getting for all this money that we are paying and for all this money that we are spending".
Government Orders
I can understand fully why my constituents feel that they are not getting value for money. When they know the government is spending 35 cents of every dollar on interest, they know full well they are not getting a dollar's worth of value for the dollar in taxes they are paying.
For example I have here the most recent statistics that relate to income tax paid by my constituents. This is personal income tax. In the town of Pickering in 1987 my constituents paid $213 million in federal income tax. In 1988 they paid $248 million in federal income tax. And they can say: "What did we get for that $35 million more in income tax that we paid?"
One thing we know we did get-we got a debt that went up. We got a deficit that did not come down, and we did not get very many new programs, but we did get an awful lot of people screaming about the fact that some of the programs they wanted were being cut, et cetera.
I can tell you that the people of Pickering object to paying an extra $35 million. The people of Whitby increased the taxes they pay from $181 million in 1987 to $217 million in 1988. Obviously with inflation that number went up again in 1989 and in 1990. So the people of Whitby can say; well, what did we get for that extra $39 million? They have every right to ask that question, and have every right to be disappointed when they can say that all they got for it was an increase in the debt, no reduction in the deficit, with those appropriate spending increases.
Similarly, in the town of Ajax the same scenario happened, where they paid an extra $23 million in income tax, and yet all they got for it was an increase in the national debt.
So, this budget deals very clearly with an issue that is important to us all. The issue is, as Mr. McKenna rightfully points out, that we cannot leave this debt to our children to pay.
So, how have we decided to address it? Certainly in this budget one of the very clear things we have done is we have put a cap on spending. I happened to listen to the member from Beaver River a little while back who was saying that this budget rates a five out of ten, and she was very critical of the fact that there were cuts made today that should have been made maybe three or four

Government Orders
years ago. Well, like her, I am a reasonably new member of Parliament and I like to participate in what I think are appropriate cuts. I listened to her speech and all I heard her say was that we did not cut enough. Last year when I listened to her I heard her say that we did not cut enough but she did not have suggestions of what should be cut; but she did complain about some of the things that were cut in her part of Canada that she did not agree with.
We all have to look at it now. We have to come up with some very concrete suggestions, we also have to come up with methods of getting ourselves off this debt treadmill. Very clearly, because of the way the government spends money, the best way to get ourselves off this debt treadmill is to increase the over-all revenues-not by increasing the tax rate, as our friends in the NDP would have us do, not by spending more money, as our friends in both the NDP and the Liberal Party would have us do, but by increasing the wealth of Canada.
That is why I was kind of pleased to see the member for Willowdale talk about how we could increase the wealth of Canada.
I understand we are in a recession today. My riding, like every other riding in Canada, is experiencing that. It is not very comfortable when you talk to people who have, for one reason or another, been laid off or lost their job; these are difficult times. But so that there should be no doubt about the fact that spending does not solve the problem, if we go back to 1981-82, the Liberal Party, the government of the day, spent, spent, spent, and raised the deficit tremendously.
If spending is the cure, then in Ontario we should today be riding the biggest boom that could possibly exist in Canada, because for the last five years the Government of Ontario has done a bigger job of spending than the federal government did when they were last in government with the Liberal Party in 1981-82. The fact of the matter is that we suffer the recession in Ontario, even though we have the biggest spending government that ever existed in Canada, right in the province of Ontario-and we have not even got a budget from the NDP yet.
So, we will certainly see how to spend money, and it is certainly proven that that is not the answer.
The answer is to create wealth by reducing the inflation rate, by reducing the over-all impact of government in the economy, and by making sure that the money the governments gets in its revenue is put towards the debt and the deficit.
In our budget we have done that. We have established an expenditure control program to control how government spends money; we have put in place a mandatory spending limit on the government so that it cannot create new and wonderful programs; and third, we have made sure that all the revenue from GST goes to reducing the debt, exactly what Canadians want and ask for.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to my colleague with great interest. However, what our colleague the Minister of Labour said in support of the federal budget seems of greater interest as former mayor of Ville d'Anjou, and as a Quebecer. I find that the budget the hon. Minister of Finance tabled is one that can be described as full of inconsistencies, thoughtless and showing incompetence. Those are not my words, mind you. They are from Le Devoir.
I find rather incredible to hear the Minister of Labour, a Quebecer, speak in support of a budget which, based on the information I have here and with the freeze on the transfer payments to the provinces, will affect mostly Quebec, particularly in the fields of health and postsecondary education. According to the Quebec Minister of Finance, Mr. Speaker, it is $732 million that we will loose over the next three years.
I hope that the Minister of Labour heard me, because he was suggesting that a budget stealing- I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, but that is the right word, "stealing" $732 million from the province of Quebec, and we have a Quebecer defending this Budget. I find that hard to take. I find that very hard to take, even if they don't agree, all these people on the other side, the Tory defenders of the rights of Quebecers: the right to be poor!
Another interesting point is that according to the same Minister of Finance, the Wilson Budget will cut about $153 million for the 1992-93 fiscal year alone. And who is that going to affect?

Not the NDP?
March 6, 1991

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
No. It is going to affect everybody. Oh, sure, the NDP too. How? But the NDP represents everybody! We represent Quebecers, we represent the people from western Canada and the people from Ontario. Even the Ontario Government will be affected.
I am going to try and get the attention of the former Minister of Labour, because I find it very interesting that a former mayor of Ville d'Anjou would agree with Mr. Wilson's Budget, when he knows perfectly well that every single municipality in Quebec will have to pay the bill, because the federal bill is being sent to the province and the province is going to send it to the municipalities. And all the mayors of Quebec's municipalities are up in arms. They are mad as hell at the government. And I don't blame them. I don't blame Marcel Dulude, the mayor of Saint-Bruno, who complained about these cutbacks which mean he will have to spend more and more money on public transit.
So if we can't pay the federal bill and we can't pay the provincial bill, we can't put all this right on the backs of the taxpayers, but that is what is happening.
I would like to talk about this Budget in connection with the Minister of Labour, because in fact, I can't see how, as Minister of Labour, he can defend a budget that caps wage increases in the public sector at 3 per cent. I would like to quote from an editorial in Le Devoir which says that Ottawa's fight against the astronomical deficit and inflation means that all governments must co-operate very closely. Co-operation, not the confrontation we have today.
We heard the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who said: Come on, we are not going to kill health insurance. We are not going to do that. And then we heard the Quebec Minister of Health, Mr. Cote, who said: It most certainly will kill health care- So I fail to understand how a Minister of Labour can say that wages of public servants should be capped, when he knows perfectly well that as mayor of VUle d'Anjou he would never have dared to freeze his employees' salaries at 3 per cent. But he is a minister now, so he can preach what he never practiced. I think that is incredible. Especially at a time when we have a government in Quebec that will never take the advice of the Tory government, which is saying: Now listen, we capped at 3 per cent so you do the same in Quebec. Come on! We have a little more compassion. We can't let the Public Service bear the brunt of the recession. That is just not right! I can
Government Orders
understand that the Minister of Labour has to stand by the government, but I was expecting him to display a touch more courage.
In closing, Mr. Speaker-I will conclude quickly, believe it or not, because time is running out-I was looking for the best way to illustrate tonight the iniquities and ill effects of the Wilson budget. What would the best illustration be?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate having the opportunity to rise and participate in the debate on Bill C-97, the borrowing authority legislation. This bill is before the House as part of the legislation flowing from the budget speech delivered last week by my esteemed colleague, the Hon. Michael Wilson, Minister of Finance.
Before I delve into the main part of my presentation, I would briefly like to cover the main highlights of the budget.
All the money from the GST will be used to reduce the deficit and then to pay down the federal debt: no new taxes for new spending for five years, ceilings will be put on federal spending and guaranteed by a new law. this is a first. Wages of MPs, cabinet ministers, the Prime Minister and civil servants are being tightly constrained and I am quite sure that the Canadian public will jump for joy at that particular item in the budget.
Transfer payments to the provinces will be limited. There will be no federal money for the ballet opera house in Toronto, a saving of some $88 million.
There will be no money now for the proposed $45 million cultural centre in Montreal, and I know that will be widely acclaimed by most Canadians. There will be spending cuts of $15 billion spread over the next five years.
Hundreds of millions of dollars in grants and contributions to special interest groups and businesses are being cut. Inflation and interest rates will fall. The deficit this year and next year will be $30.5 billion, dropping to $6.5 billion by 1994. There will be new assistance for the disabled.
Civil servant wage increases are being capped at 3 per cent, and there will be a possible elimination of 6,000 more public servant jobs. There will be a 10 per cent cut in the number of executives in the government.
The government will attempt to create a partnership of all levels of government to deal with the rising costs of governments and attack unnecessary overlap and duplication.
The budget's priority is action to create the essential conditions for economic recovery. As a responsible government, we have chosen not to increase spending. Frankly, history has shown that throwing money at a problem or situation does not work.
My hon. friends across the floor on the Liberal benches would be more aware of that fact than any of us. After all, successive Liberal governments measured problem solving by how many of the taxpayers' dollars could be expended at any given time.
It was a practice that burdened the Canadian people with a $38.4 billion deficit in the last year of the Liberal regime in 1984, just before we came into office and formed the government. It is a practice that the February 26 budget is designed to remedy once and for all. In fact, for the first time in Canadian history, Ottawa is actually going to pass a law which puts ceilings on how much politicians can spend.
However, it should be noted that regardless of what the opposition parties tell the people, we are not a heartless government. Spending for the unemployed in the budget has been increased by $3 billion, by $1.6 billion for senior citizens, $1.3 billion for farmers in difficulty and another $600 million for our Department of National Defence.
Since being elected in 1984, our government has waged a long and determined battle to restore health to Canada's finances and stop the debt from dragging down the economy. In the 1990 budget, the government set out a medium-term fiscal plan to sharply reduce the deficit and curtail new government borrowing in financial markets by 1994 and 1995. The February 26 budget reaffirms the plan and introduces a program of expenditure control.
We have seen how living beyond our country's means can lead to a growing burden of public debt. In 1984, the federal government was handing out $1.33 in programs and services for every dollar it collected. That was certainly no bargain.
March 6, 1991

Today, our public debt is forecast to reach the staggering sum of $400 billion by mid-year, about $15,000 for every man, woman and child in Canada. The interest alone on the debt will eat up more than $43 million next year, more than we spend on Old Age Security, unemployment insurance and family allowances combined.
In the February 26 budget the government has asked Canadians to share the burden of further fiscal restraint. As a government we recognize the sacrifices that many Canadians have already made in the name of restraint. We know there is reluctance to accept the necessity for more of the same. But as bitter as the pill seems, if we took no steps to deal with this worsening fiscal situation, the deficit would be much higher than forecast over the next five years and an additional $25 billion would be added to the public debt.
I do not believe for one minute that Canadians really want to continue on a path which not only mortgages their future, but the future of subsequent generations. In the budget the government has taken the tough responsible decisions necessary to ensure Canada's finances become healthy again.
The government's plan for economic recovery seeks to ensure spending control that will help put government finances firmly on the course to a balanced budget. In fact, the 1991 budget includes measures providing Canadians with added assurance that these targets will be met. In a significant change that alters the way government manages its expenditures, it is my understanding that draft legislation will be released shortly which will impose mandatory limits on annual program spending for the next five years. The budget's program spending control measures will be enforced by law. Flexibility will be confined to a very limited set of contingencies set out in the legislation. Although the legislation will not preclude new programs to meet new needs, the government will fund new programs from within the total legislated spending ceiling of roughly 3 per cent per year.
The government will also introduce legislation to set up a debt servicing and reduction fund. The fund will receive the net revenues from the goods and services tax, net proceeds from privatization and earmarked contributions for debt reductions from individuals or businesses. These revenues will be applied first against the cost of
Government Orders
servicing the debt and as they grow over time they will be used to reduce the outstanding debt.
In combination with the proposed annual spending limits, this fund will provide assurance that all revenues from the GST will be used to service and reduce the debt and not to fund new program spending. The effort to reduce spending and the deficit is being reinforced by the government's decision to set clear inflation targets. These targets will serve as realistic goals to encourage lower inflationary expectations by all sectors of our economy: consumers, business, labour, investors and all levels of government. This will help us work together to better control the price and wage pressures that push inflation higher for us all.
There can be no denying the direct link between inflation and interest rates. Our economic history proves it. During the 1950s and 1960s, when inflation was low, averaging less than 3 per cent a year, interest rates were low also. When inflation surged in the 1970s interest rates also soared.
The rewards of lower inflation are clear and concrete. Interest rates will drop, economic productivity and competitiveness will increase, our standard of living will rise, and social fairness will be enhanced. The result will be a strong, more prosperous country that can ensure its place as an economic world leader.
Through the plan for economic recovery contained in the budget, the federal government is taking action to establish fiscal stability and strengthen confidence in Canada's future. By reducing the deficit and controlling the public debt, the plan will help set the stage for improved economic performance and increased prosperity. I believe the plan will result in a better balance between fiscal and monetary policy, and will provide the lower interest rates and greater confidence that will fuel our economic recovery.
With all this in mind, let me mention that Bill C-97 requests borrowing authority in the amount of $28.4 billion. While this is a very large amount, it is important to remember that without the strong measures contained in the budget, it would be some $4 billion to $5 billion larger.
I am pleased to support this bill on behalf of the government.

March 6, 1991
Government Orders

What I cannot accept is the government throwing up its hands in the air, passing the problems onto the provinces, the sick, the unemployed, the homeless or the students who are in charge of our future.
Not only have Canadians been asked to make sacrifices, they cannot even be sure that the sacrifices this government is asking them to make will actually do as much good as the government claims.
There is plenty of evidence, in previous budgets for example, to suggest that this budget's projections for the deficit and the interest rate for inflation are a way off base. This lack of credibility makes it very hard for Canadians to accept the medicine that this government is forcing on them.
During January and February, the Liberal task force on the economy held hearings all across this country. We held hearings because we wanted to hear, firsthand, what Canadians had to say about the state of the economy, about their own particular situation and we wanted to listen to any suggestions they had.
We went to approximately 35 communities across this country from North River, Prince Edward Island to northern Ontario, from London, Ontario to Vancouver, British Columbia. We listened, we took notes, and we will use that material from these hearings as we develop our own economic policies.
The input this task force received on Prince Edward Island was extremely useful, providing what might be called a yardstick against which this government's budget may be compared.
This 1991 federal budget cuts across a wide variety of interests, from students to small business, from low income housing to the environment. The largest cut to my province of Prince Edward Island, in terms of dollars, was obviously in the transfer payments for education and health.
To give a little bit of background, the previous Liberal government in 1977 concluded an agreement with the provinces, whether they would pay each province so much per capita based on how the economy was growing.
Not long after taking office, this government decided that it would change that, so it limited transfers to the provinces at first by a couple of percentage points. Then, it froze the transfers of cash altogether. That freeze continues to this day and it will continue according to this budget until 1996.
This latest budget wipes out over $2 billion in support for provincial health and education. In terms of Prince Edward Island, the 1991 budget trims approximately $17 million of Prince Edward Island's potential budget for education and health for the next three years alone.
March 6, 1991

This lost revenue from Ottawa has to be picked up somewhere. The province has to do that either by increasing taxes, or by reducing services. It has to get the money somewhere. Maybe, it will mean that the universities will have to increase tuition fees.
More important than the money is what reduced spending on education will mean to the future of the province and the country. How important is education? I want to quote a well-known politician:
People are Canada's most important resource. That is why we are
going to focus more and more of our attention and resources on
long-term investment in people, education, literacy and the
upgrading of skills.
That is a quote from Prime Minister Brian Mulroney, speaking in Calgary, April 5, 1990.
I know that my time is getting short. I just want to end by saying that Canadians are looking to their national government for leadership and especially during times like this; times of recession and especially when our national future is at stake, this need becomes even greater. But what this government has shown again in the budget, is that it is unable to provide that leadership.
Canadians expect better. Canadian deserves better. After the next election and the swearing in of a new Liberal government, Canadians will receive better.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I also wish to join the debate this evening on the budget.
This budget is a continuation of all the previous budgets introduced by this Minister of Finance and the government. I am afraid he was wrong when he first introduced a budget after being elected to the government in 1984, as he is wrong today. It is a wrong attitude; it is a wrong philosophy; it is a wrong direction. I think the results of each of the budgets have indicated how wrong the direction of the government is.
Rather than reducing deficits, we have seen our deficits grow until now, in terms of our accumulated deficit, it is well over $400 billion. We have seen our taxes increase, particularly the taxes of ordinary Canadian men and women. We have seen government services, public services being drastically reduced, budget after budget after budget. It is a downscaling of government. A tremendous redistribution of wealth is occur-
Govemment Orders
ring, because it means that ordinary working people are paying more and getting less.
As a New Democrat, I have no objection to fighting the deficit. As a New Democrat, I see the interest payments we pay every year as a redistribution of wealth to the more well-to-do. Because it is only the banks, financial institutions and those individuals who hold bonds that benefit from our deficit. We see a distribution of billions of dollars every year from the public coffers to those individuals. So fighting the deficit is no problem for me.
To be sure, it is a problem that was created by the Liberal regime, particularly when Mr. Tbmer was the Minister of Finance. They thought they would have the quick fix by allowing all sorts of tax deductions for large corporations, assuming that the extra wealth the corporations would get would be reinvested and create more jobs, expand plants and create more wealth.
We knew back then it did not work quite that way. Unfortunately, the Tories are even more so committed to the notion of the trickle-down theory, of giving special tax breaks and concessions to the wealthy and to the large corporations while fighting the deficit on the backs of the elderly, the young, working men and women, farmers and fishermen of this country.
It is wrong. It is morally wrong and it is economically wrong. It makes no sense whatsoever.
The Minister of Finance has charged that New Democrats just bicker and we do not have any solutions. Well, we do have solutions. I was on the finance committee when we went through the process of tax reform and, out of that process, the New Democratic Party presented a report on tax reform, which is our solutions to the problems.
At that time I also stated, both in committee and publicly, that if we are going to have genuine tax reform in this country, we must also have a measure of political reform. If we are going to have genuine tax reform it should be done by including all of the political parties, working together to come up with a tax scheme that would be fair and effective.
The Minister of Finance rejected our proposals, as he rejected the many excellent proposals of the finance committee itself. This Minister of Finance, in his stub-

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
bomness, his Department of Finance with the bureaucrats in their stubbornness, insisted that the proposals they had laid forward in tax reform were it or nothing else. In that proposal they made many projections.
I remember how the Minister of Finance assured us in committee that he had plugged up the loopholes that resulted in not one major life insurance company in this country paying a cent of tax for over a decade. He assured us that he had plugged up the loopholes that saw, for example, in a case in 1983 of one bank where a teller at that bank paid more actual dollars and cents in taxes than the bank did, even though the bank had over $300-some million in profits.
However, when the figures came in and the real world was discovered, the insurance companies and the banks had found other ways in and around his regulations and they were no good. He had to finally back down and accept some of the proposals that were made by the finance committee.
Had the Minister of Finance heeded the advice, and had we, on the finance committee, been able to come forward with a package of genuine tax reform, including the reform of the sales tax and the corporate tax as well as the income tax, it would not have been a package that all the Conservatives, all the Liberals and all the New Democrats would have been happy with, but it would have been a package that would have had the political commitment of all the political parties behind it and it would have been a package that would have ensured fairness in our tax system.
Instead, tax reform has been a dismal failure of this government. Rather than plugging up those loopholes, we see the amount of taxes being paid by the corporate sector, but particularly certain segments of the corporate sector, i.e. the financial institutions and the real estate developers still not paying their fair share of taxes.
Let me come back to the point I mentioned earlier. I have no problem fighting the deficit; indeed, we have to reduce the deficit. But let us reduce the deficit in a fair and equitable manner. The record of this government is its unfairness as it tackles the problem of the deficit.
We see in this budget a further erosion of medicare and further cutbacks which will affect our post-secondary education. These are investments in the country. These are investments in the future, particularly postsecondary education. It means that our youngsters will have less of an opportunity in the future. It means what this Minister of Finance calls down-scaling, passing on the burden to the provinces. The provinces in turn will cut back and pass the burden on to municipalities.
This country has developed marvellous social programs in health and education over the years. Often it was this party forcing the Liberals when they were in the minority situation to enact certain progressive steps. But the aim of this government is to destroy all of that. And for what? What are we to be left with? We have a country in ruin. We have political dissent and economic chaos. We have people unemployed. There is no sense of confidence in the economy of this country. Our infrastructure is being depleted. Our education system, our post-secondary education institutions are crumbling. There is no sense of hope and future and confidence by Canadians. That is the result of the budgets of the Minister of Finance.
For heaven's sake, Minister of Finance, for the sake of Canadians, for the sake of the future, resign.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to be here on this very nice night.
I want to speak to this borrowing bill which fits into this government's whole economic agenda. It is an agenda that is leading us down the road to deconfederation.
At the same time that peace in the Persian Gulf is around the comer, if it is not actually here already, this Conservative government has decided to declare war on Canada and the people of Canada, the unemployed and the regions of Canada that are really very hard hit by this recession.
This Conservative government has allowed Canada to drift. Not only has it allowed it to drift, but it has actually admitted to causing this first made-in-Canada recession, and this budget does absolutely nothing to help our economy back on track.
We understand that the deficit is a very serious problem and the debt is a very serious problem. We have no problem in dealing with that. But what we are worried about is how can one deal with that kind of a deficit and a debt when there are no jobs, when corporations, especially small businesses are all losing their shirts, they are

Government Orders
not paying any tax and, therefore, the deficit will grow even larger.
This government has practically strangled employment opportunities as a result of maintaining high interest rates and a high dollar. This government has introduced the GST, an expensive and very complex tax which is also very regressive, especially for the regions of the country. It increases inflation. As a matter of fact, in January we had a very massive increase in inflation.
Now that this government has brought us into this recession-by its own admission, they tell us it was a planned recession- it has turned its back on us. At a time when the government predicts that unemployment will rise to 10 per cent, the government has cut spending on job creation and has increased unemployment insurance premiums. If there was one area in which I would have liked to have seen some government interference it would have been in job creation projects.
I come from the riding of Sudbury. In the early 1980s when this country went through a very serious recession, we probably were the hardest hit of all the regions of the country. We had unemployment rates in excess of 28 to 30 per cent of our population. I was a business person in the community at that time. They were terrible, terrible times. But I must say that the government intervened; government helped us out. Today, Sudbury is a very viable community; actually, we are probably one of the bright spots of the country.
I would say to the people on the government side that that is because the government invested dollars, and the dollars invested at that time have now produced tremendous benefits. We are now paying our own way now and we are very happy to do so. The thing that bothers us is that we see this government turning its back on other areas that might need it very much.
Ultimately, it is the Canadian taxpayer who will pay for the Conservative mismanagement of our economy. Canadian employees and businesses are being made to pay more in unemployment insurance premiums now that the government no longer contributes to the unemployment insurance program.
In addition, the provinces and municipalities will either pass on the pain to their taxpayers or they will drastically reduce services that the federal government is now refusing to pay for.
The Minister of Finance now expects Canadians to trust his budget and his fiscal policies to bring Canada out of the economic doldrums and into prosperity. After almost seven years in office during which Canada shared with the rest of the western economies almost unprecedented economic growth and despite having resorted to 30, 32 or 33 different tax increases, paid largely by the middle and lower income Canadians, the Minister of Finance has failed in bringing the deficit under control. In fact, he has managed to double the federal debt while at the economic control.
This is the same Minister of Finance who told Canadians in 1985 that the deficit in 1991 would be $18 billion. Last week, he announced that he was really doing a good job because he was going to hold it at $30.5 billion over the next couple of years. How can we believe his prediction? He says one thing, but the next year he revises all the time.
This is also the same Minister of Finance who told us the GST would have a minimal impact on inflation. Inflation in January jumped to 6.8 per cent, the largest increase in inflation in 33 years. Now he expects Canadians to believe that inflation will be at 3.2 per cent in 1992 and he predicts interest rates at 9 per cent. How, pray tell, can he have inflation at 3.2 per cent if interest rates are still that high?
The Minister of Finance continues to insist that his fiscal policies are necessary to ensure Canada's competitiveness in international markets. How can Canadian businesses compete under this Minister of Finance's high interest rate, high dollar economic policies? What happened to the Prime Minister's pledge to invest in Canada's future?
Canada's future lies in research and development, and in the education of our young people. How can we compete when the government is cutting funding for post-secondary education, and research and development? The Tories have attacked the bonds that hold us together as a nation. Our social programs are among the only things that bind us together now from coast to coast.

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
At a time when the government should be strengthening national unity, it is weakening what is considered to be one of the best national social safety nets in the world.
It has made drastic cuts to national institutions such as the CBC, and now the Prime Minister seems prepared to give away more and more of the federal government's powers to the province.
Let me get back to the CBC. The government always tells us that it is cutting these things to save money. Now, we have just heard with the Supplementary Estimates that it is going to cost $48 million because of the cuts that it made last time around. It is not really saving any money. It is just destroying the country, because everything it does seems to cost a lot more than it predicts.
The only thing that this budget has succeeded in doing is to pit public servants and Canadians in general one against the other. Someone once said that the true moral test of government is how it treats those in the dawn of life, the children. There is nothing in this budget for the children. In fact, it will increase their poverty. There is no day care. There is absolutely no consideration to these people in our community.
The true moral test of government is how it treats those who are in the twilight of life, the aged. This government has clawed back on old age pensions. Name it. It would do much worse if the Canadian people had let it. Because of one lady in particular who said: "No more, Charlie Brown. No way, Charlie Brown," it decided to change its mind. It is still continuing when we think of medicare. That will really hurt those who most need it.
The true moral test of government is how it treats those who are in the shadow of life; the sick, the needy, the disadvantaged. Just think in terms of what this government is doing to things like welfare programs. It may not be doing it directly, but it is asking the provinces to do its dirty work for them.
It is asking the civil servants to turn against their own co-workers, to decide whether they should have an increase in their wages. Heaven help us. We are all faced with the same increases; they are also. They have to choose between giving themselves an increase or firing their brother. What kind of a government is so heartless that it would ask someone to do that, instead of doing
and making the decisions itself. I would think that this government would have the guts to stand up and say that it perhaps does not need this particular department. If that is what it wants to do, then do it.
This government has 46 ministries. Why does any government in Canada need 46 ministries, or 43 ministries, or whatever the number is? In the United States they have 10 or 15 ministries and they have a population that so far outranks ours that it is unbelievable. If they can do it with 10 or 15 ministers, why can't we? Let's practise what we preach and let's do something for Canadians and not just the idea of what Conservatives can do for themselves.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to speak for a short time on the borrowing bill. What I would like to do is to attack this from the perspective of a number of other speeches that I have made in the just over two years that I have been a member of this House; and that is from the angle of what is happening to our country, what I have seen happening to the country, and what the people that I have spoken to across the country have told me is happening to the country, in their minds.
Let me quote from the budget speech, starting where the Finance Ministers tells us right off the bat that:
- this is a strong budget-a budget for economic recovery.
He then goes on to say that:
Our Plan for Economic Recovery is different from those in previous recessions.
And he finally concludes by saying:
We all wish to see a strong, united and prosperous Canada. Our Plan for Economic Recovery will help us achieve that goal.
It saddens me to have to say that what I have seen in this budget is a continuation of those policies that have ripped the guts out of everything in Canada that all of us have grown to love and cherish.
I would like to read some sections from an article in The Globe and Mail, written by Geoffrey York. In that, the Roman Catholic bishops warn that:
An economic transformation is turning Canada into a "deeply fragmented and polarized society" whose people are divided against themselves.
I will come back to that statement in a couple of minutes. They further say that:
March 6, 1991

The shift to low-paying, part-time jobs is transforming Canada into a society polarized "between rich and poor, urban and rural, women and men, older and younger workers, white and non-white".
They further say that:
This is worsening the phenomenon of the gap between the rich and the poor.
And finally, Tony Clarke, director of the social affairs department of the Catholic bishops, said:
-ordinary Canadians have felt one blow after another. This week's federal budget will probably worsen the situation for working people in Canada."
They said the government has "largely abandoned job creation efforts, while cutting social programs and reducing transfer payments for health, education and social assistance."
The bishops in that are dead on the mark. That is exactly what we have seen in the three budgets that I have debated in this House. It is the policies that started with the Conservatives taking power in 1984 and have continued, where the policies of this government are established by the wealthy, the 5 per cent of the wealthy, the poor get poorer and the middle class, as has been shown by StatsCanada in a recent study by the Fraser Institute, are paying more and more in taxation. Their actual after-tax income is dropping substantially. Everything points to the widening of that gap.
I said that I would return to the shift to low-paying part-time jobs. What we have seen, and we talk of job creation when we come to this place, we hear the government constantly telling us how many jobs they have created, and what seems to be happening is more and more of the industrial jobs seem to be either drying up or moving south of the border. More and more we are getting into the service-oriented jobs, the "McJobs", the jobs that are lower paying. The incomes are falling. The young people with families are having a harder time getting employment that is able to keep their family to any type of a standard of living. Some of these younger families are forced to have two jobs, three jobs, and four jobs just trying to keep up with their every day and day-to-day expenses.
What this government has done is heap upon them the goods and services tax. Now in this budget after getting hit with that we have increases in unemployment insurance, cutbacks in the Canada Assistance Plan, capping of that particular plan, the Established Programs Financing. All of these filter down, part of what has been or appears to be the plan, and has been the plan I would suggest, for the six years that this government has been in power.
Government Orders
What happens when the unemployment insurance rates go up? What happens when there is capped funding on the Canada Assistance Plan or the Established Programs Financing? Well, we either cut back on the programs or we force the provinces and the municipalities to increase their taxes.
Once again, who gets hit by those taxes? Who does not have tax breaks? Well it is the middle-income and the lower-income people. If the province passes these on to the municipalities then it is the property owners who end up paying once again.
Interestingly enough, the unemployment insurance increases hit directly at those property owners and renters in all municipalities across Canada and particularly in rural Canada. The biggest employers in small towns such as Osoyoos, Oliver, Okanagan Falls, Penticton, Summerland; places in my riding, Grand Forks, Princeton, Merritt, are the hospitals, the school districts, and the municipalities.
They have to get their money. They cannot deficit finance as the federal government has done. They have to have their money up front and they have to get their money through property taxation. Who foots the bill for the property taxes in rural Canada? Well, it is usually the middle-income and lower-income people through rent and through property taxes, once again whittling that away.
Also getting hit in this is the small business community and I think as we all know, as has been said time and again in the House and by others, 80 per cent of the employment over the last 10 years has been created by the small business community.
And what has happened to them in this budget? Once again, falling to them will be increases in unemployment insurance. The GST has hit them and hit them strong and hard.
In my riding tourism is a major industry. We know that tourism has already started to fall off and will fall continuously. In the area next to the border the perception that is out there of the added cost is forcing people down below the borders to shop, again hurting the small business retailers in the riding of Okanagan-Similka-meen-Merritt, all through the Okanagan as a matter of

Government Orders
fact, and I would suggest all across Canada within 100 miles of the border at least.
One thing that hits hard and hits hard at all of us is cuts in Canadian Jobs Strategy. These are programs that we have used well in rural Canada. They have helped us at times of high unemployment. In my riding the unemployment rate is approximately 17 per cent adjusted, unadjusted substantially higher than that. But we use these programs and use them very effectively to assist people in retraining, to re-enter the job market. That is being cut, and being cut substantially.
What we have seen in this budget is more pie in the sky. Our Minister of Finance tells us: "We are going to get inflation down. We are going to fight inflation. We want to see a strong and united Canada". Well, what we have here is a formula for failure. A formula for failure politically. A formula for failure economically and a formula for failure socially.
We will continue to speak out, present alternatives and speak out very strongly against this government's attack on the middle-income, low-income earners and on the poor.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I really appreciate this opportunity to address the borrowing authority bill before the House. It really is a mechanism that begins the process of implementing this government's policy, this government's budget policy and this government's expression and vision for the future. In a sense, when you see and read this budget, it expresses the narrow ideological, market-driven agenda of this government. It does not in any way, even pretend to respond to the real needs of the ordinary people out there in the countryside; the woman who is concerned about child care, the women who is on the job market and worried about whether she is going to still have a job, the man in his mid-forties to early fifties who has built a career and now finds that his job is gone and he is out of sync with the needs and qualifications called for in the marketplace. That is the ordinary bread and butter issue. Can I pay my mortgage rates? Can I meet my car payment? Have I enough money, if I am in a different bracket, to pay for my RRSP? All the ordinary things that ordinary people think about and worry about and we
often forget about, standing here talking in this House of Commons.
At some point, in the few minutes that I have, I want to address some of the issues around the cultural sector. I just wanted to bring to the attention of the House that it is unfortunate, but this is not a budget of hope. It is not a budget delivered at the right time with the right message. It is a budget that tries to put the brakes on an economy that is already in a tailspin. It is a budget that steps backward in many, many areas, and fails to address, as I say, the ordinary needs of the people of this country in a balanced way and deal with the social inequities that have come about through a number of issues; whether it was the free trade agreement that has not given us a level playing field, whether it is the made-in-Canada recession or whether it is a very poor tax policy that has increased taxes unconscionably on middle income earners, pushing them down towards the lower-income level.
When you have a policy that has a high interest rate and has kept our dollar ridiculously high and then expect to have our people compete, both nationally and internationally, and do not give people the skills they require, I ask: What is expected and what kind of a message is this government sending to the country?
The lack of investment in Canadian research and development, the lack of any kind of commitment to transfer of technology when we deal with countries which come in here to do business, without any commitment to put back into this wonderful society that this government inherited, is a pretty sad lack of vision and condemnation of the lack of foresight of the leadership across this floor.
How are we supposed to be dealing with these social inequities in this budget? The last seven years have been really nice, healthy growing years for the economy and for business. People have done well. Yet, during this time of prosperity, we have not been able to work down our national deficit and accumulated debt. When we were not able to do this in the fat years, if I may call them that, and now we want to try and do it during the lean years, it seems to me that there is a peculiar mental block in this government about figuring out the priorities at the right time and in the right way.
March 6, 1991

If the government could not address the social inequities at a time of prosperity, do you think this is the time to do it? If it did not address them then, when will it?
The budget was the opportune moment to right some of the wrongs this government committed. I fear that the moment has been lost. It has not in any way indicated any desire to rebuild the infrastructure that it has cut to pieces-VIA Rail, Air Canada, Petro-Canada, all those things that linked this country-or the CBC, which it has systematically destroyed over the last seven years.
Then we move to the GST, a tax that the Canadian people did not want. They said it time and time again; every Gallup Poll showed they did not want this tax. It was not the idea of taxes. People understand that to have social programs, to have social contracts, to do certain things in arts and culture, they have to pay taxes, that the money has to come from somewhere.
To have the money come from imposing a tax that is so regressive, that is so hurtful, that brought about increased inflation, that is ridiculous in some of its in and out administration, that put 3,000 new people in there and has caught the eyes and ears of the world, how on earth can Canadians have any confidence in a finance minister and a government that plan in this way?
I say to you it has imposed a tax that is unconscionable. In supplementary spending estimates there is a requirement for $180 million to complete the implementation of this tax. In fact, if you look at the $559 million extra in supplementary spending that was just tabled by the minister, you will see that the biggest chunk of new money is for the GST.
The Department of National Revenue receives an extra $153.5 million for planning and administering the tax, while the Department of Public Works receives an additional $24.5 million to provide GST related office space, and the Department of Finance receives an extra $2.3 million for GST inquiries and communications. Add that to the $365.8 million in GST related spending in the Supplementary Estimates last November, and yesterday's estimates bring the cost of planning and implementing the GST and the related tax credit for low income Canadians in 1990 to a total of $546.1 million.
Government Orders
That is more than double the estimate of $260 million in GST administration costs that were included in the February 1990 budget. I think it is absolutely scandalous.
What do we have from the seven-year term of this Conservative government, as reflected in this budget, but a national debt that has now doubled, as I already talked about, and very high inflation.
This government said that it, when it took power, would make the economy more competitive. But we have slipped dramatically in the OECD ratings and lost hundreds of thousands of manufacturing jobs, including hundreds, maybe thousands in my own riding.
There is nothing new in this budget to give people who are hurting any hope. The food banks are busier than ever, people are losing homes and businesses, and families are struggling to make ends meet; and this government has the nerve to tell us that Canadians ought to toughen up, stay the course, tighten their belts. It makes me wonder what world the government is living in.
I had wanted to address the government's cut of $100 million to the Canadian Jobs Strategy program, to talk about its watering down of the funding for the green plan-so much for environmental commitment, which is the concern for tomorrow. I wanted to talk about the 15 per cent cut in social housing, which I consider heartless, and the increase of UI premiums again-that is a tax increase. I think it is up 24 per cent, although that could be an inaccurate figure.
To top it all off, this has followed six years of prosperity. All in all, I would suggest to our young people looking to go into the marketplace that there is not much hope at this moment. We have cut money in all those areas and we have cut investment in research and development. This budget dashes hopes for many, many thousands of Canadians.
Let us look at the cultural dossier for a couple of minutes. Looking at it you can really become heartsick. Canadians deserve better. The culture of a country defines it on the international map, on the global world stage.
The cultural community is in the forefront of the development of all nations, this nation no more and no less than any other nation. It is an area for innovation, creativity and resourcefulness. I suggest to you that this

Government Orders
is what is lacking in terms of the vision this country should have, that this budget should have for cultural development.
I am not going to talk about the savaging of the CBC. It goes without saying. There is $45 million in the budget to help with the severance pay. Telefilm, which allows us to see ourselves on film, has been cut to the tune of $28 million over the next five years. Canada Council is frozen, and they have lost close to $20 million over the last four or five years. The ballet-opera house lost the federal government's promise of $88 million. The Edmonton concert hall, and the Montreal concert hall, those have also been cut.
I am not the least bit sorry about the $45 million in the cultural research institute because that could have gone another way.
Other budget items have been of serious concern to all of us. That $100 million from the Canadian Jobs Strategy is unconscionable at this time.
The last point I want to make is the fact that prior to the budget of the Minister of Finance the federal government had earmarked $50 million for training in the cultural sector. What is happening? What does that mean for our arts and our cultural institutions? I think that it is very sad.
I would just quote Jay Stone of The Ottawa Citizen who said: "You can tell a lot about a government by how it spends it money. In fact you can tell everything. Just follow the dollar signs to the heart of policy and a dark heart it is for those of us with some passing interest in culture, dark and mysterious, and with a slight, little murmur that might be the faraway sounds of public opinion dropping gently on the ground". It is a sad day for Canada.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1991-92 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not a budget. This is a political indictment against the aspirations of working men and women in Canada. It is an attack on the very foundations of this country and an assault on the pillars of our Canadian way of life. This budget attacks our system of universal health care, it attacks the foundations of our post-secondary educational institutions and it attacks our whole system of income assistance.
The Minister of Finance when he announced the budget said there were no new taxes. But this budget itself is a hidden tax on all working Canadians because it is a pass the buck budget. It passes it over to the provinces and it lets the provinces and the taxpayers of those individual provinces deal with the difficulties that this budget has caused. The government, through this budget, is relinquishing its own authority, almost through default, by passing its responsibility to the provinces.
With respect to unemployment insurance, last year the government announced that it was getting out of the unemployment insurance program. It passed over the responsibility of funding that program to the small business community and to the workers. When it passed the buck to the businesses and to the workers last year, the minister promised that should there be future shortfalls in the funding the government would make up the difference. But this budget puts the lie to that promise because the workers and the business community now find that they are going to have to make up that extra cost.
One hundred million dollars out of the Canadian Jobs Strategy, which is a program that works well. As my colleague from Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt was saying earlier, it creates a lot of job opportunities in areas like the interior of British Columbia, and it is a program whose funding, the minister last year assured this House, was secure. Another broken promise.
There is a lot of big talk by this government about the need to be competitive. Yet at the same time it neglects the job training skills and funding for job upgrading that will allow our workers and our young people to get the kind of training they need to be competitive in this global marketplace.
The capping of the extended program funding will force the provinces again to make up the difference. The financial assistance to the provinces for health care services and for post-secondary education was traditionally provided by the federal government. This program has been attacked time and time again in a succession of Tory budgets. In B.C. alone over the next five years we are going to lose $911 million out of post-secondary and health care funding because of the continual erosion.

The finance minister has said that a steady declining federal contribution will greatly exaggerate and aggravate the provincial problem of funding these programs.
Extending the Canada Assistance Plan 5 per cent ceiling is again passing the buck over to the provinces, forcing the provinces to make up the difference.
Some $600 million was stolen out of the green plan initiative, an initiative heralded by this government as being its commitment to environmental integrity in Canada. Now it is watering it down once again, with another $600 million being taken out of it.
There seems to be no bottom line with this government when it comes to expenditures for war, but there is certainly a bottom line for everything else. That $600 million, I understand, is going to fund the cost of the Department of National Defence in both the Oka crisis and the gulf war crisis. But why did it have to come out of the environmental initiatives?
The only sector in this country that has not been asked to make a sacrifice on the altar of restraint is the corporate sector. Not one tax break has been discontinued. Not one loophole has been closed. Not one initiative has been taken to get the corporate elite of Canada to pay its fair share.
If we had simply disallowed the deduction for business lunches, the three martini lunches, we could have saved over a billion dollars in revenue for this government. Introducing a minimum corporate tax could have reclaimed billions more.
In 1987-and these are Statistics Canada figures-93,000 profitable corporations in this country paid no taxes whatsoever on combined profits of some $27 billion, with a capital b, no tax. The government continues to be oblivious of the need for real tax reform. It does not care that the burden has been shifted to the shoulders of ordinary working men and women in Canada.
I want to point out that in 1950 individuals and corporations across this land contributed equal amounts, 50/50, to the taxes, toward Canada's coffers. Since that time the corporate share of taxation in this country has dropped to 14 per cent, whereas the tax burden for working men and women in Canada has increased to over 84 per cent.
Government Orders
When this government's friends in Canada's corporate community demand a reduction in the deficit, they never talk about shouldering more of this tax burden that they have been relieved of since 1950. No, they talk about the need to cut social spending, the need to trim health care, income assistance and unemployment insurance. The Tory government, time and time again, falls over itself in attempts to accommodate them.
Cuts to health care, cuts to unemployment insurance, cuts to post-secondary education, cuts to job training, cuts to income assistance, cuts to environmental initiatives, cuts, cuts, cuts, but never one corporate loophole closed. It is a Tory corporate agenda to harmonize our social and political system by taking it down to the market driven level of our U.S. neighbour.
When a business gets public money or a corporate bailout is needed to save another megacorporation, they call that a vital incentive, but when a single mother gets public money to help feed a child, that is a welfare frill.
Last year alone, over 160,000 jobs vanished in our manufacturing industry. Trident Limited, an auto parts manufacturer, accepted a $2 million giveaway, a grant from the federal government to help create Canadian jobs. Then what did it do? It flitted down to Tennessee and thumbed its nose at Canada in light of the free trade agreement.
From 1970 to 1975 corporate profits in this country grew 100 per cent. They more than doubled again from 1975 to 1980, and they grew by half again from 1980 to 1985. In the decade between 1975 and 1985 corporate profits in Canada totalled over $305 billion. Now they shoulder only 12 per cent or 13 per cent of the total tax burden.
What happens at the first whiff of a recession? Profits are transferred to foreign parent companies and are paid as dividends to foreign shareholders. This increased by 150 per cent the last time the economy took a tailspin. Canada is being bled by the haemorrhaging of our tax dollars to foreign investment firms.
I know my time is limited. I just want to say that there is no question at all that we have a serious debt problem in Canada. There is no question that we have to deal with it, but who caused the debt?

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
Since Confederation to 1980, our total debt was $77 billion. Four years later, under the Liberal administration, that debt had grown to $187 billion. In the last six years alone, that debt has more than doubled to almost $400 billion. There is no argument that serious efforts have to be made in debt reduction, but this government has decided in order to make that debt reduction to ram it down the throats of ordinary working men and women in Canada. Canada to this government, just in summarizing, has become a marketplace; nothing more and nothing less.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to rise in the House this very day to speak to matters of the economy of particular importance to my constituents.
As always, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak, particularly on not just matters that are of concern to my constituents, but to all Canadians.
When the budget was tabled over a week ago, I thought of how the government has mismanaged the economy for seven consecutive years. Ibday, the standard of living in Canada has subsequently declined dramatically.
I sent a communique to my constituents on February 26 shortly after the Minister of Finance presented the budget, and I told my constituents that the budget had no surprises. Indeed, services will be decreased, programs will be cut, Canadians will be paying more in taxes, and the majority of the responsibility will be placed on the provincial, territorial and municipal governments, on small businesses, on consumers and on individual Canadians least able to pay for the federal government's mistakes. The government was spending out of control during the good years when the economy was expanding and is cutting back at the worst possible time, in the midst of a deep recession.
We still have that huge deficit. None of that jiggery-pokery, the so-called high falutin fiscal policy this government has put forward, has worked. It is a shame. Even this severe Conservative agenda has not worked.
I spent the week before the budget was presented in the west and in the north, in both the Northwest Territories and in Yukon, meeting with people as part of the Liberal task force on the recession and the economy. I am privileged to have shared first-hand the concerns and struggles which Canadians are having in their effort to survive another Tory budget. It is this information that I want to share with members in this House tonight. I will put that information in perspective with this seventh consecutive budget of no hope. I feel this especially in the north since we have the highest cost of living and no initiative to boost the economy of the north.
I would like the Minister of Finance to explain to Canadians why the deficit is still increasing and public debt is now out of control. All this government spending has produced nothing in new initiatives. There is no National Energy Strategy, no areas for job creation which would help to stimulate the economy, the environmental green plan is being delayed-this will have a detrimental impact on the north-there is no child care strategy-a promise Canadians have been waiting for since 1984, there is no regional development plan, and no money for training, nor research and development.
There are wage controls at a time when the cost of living is at a record high. This will be hard on northern workers. Trade unions will be threatened with job losses. The Arctic environment strategy will be delayed as may be the Canadian Polar Commission. Social housing and CMHC programs are reduced which will directly affect aboriginal people across Canada. Health programs and welfare and post-secondary education moneys are reduced. As usual, the poor people, the aboriginal people, and those unable to afford these reductions will be punished.
The budget does nothing to tackle the recession or to stimulate economic growth, and it does nothing for northerners. There is no recognition of the potential that the Arctic can contribute. The desperate need for northern infrastructure and the excessively high cost of living in the north have been ignored by the Mulroney government for the seventh budget in succession.
In the north the north engineering sustainable economic development in small northern communities is an enormous problem. Last night my colleague from Nu-
March 6, 1991

natsiaq delivered his debate on the budget and described the monumental economic problems that northerners are confronting on a daily basis, really as a way of life.
My riding is the largest in North America, second only to my colleague from Nunatsiaq. In mid-February we travelled together from the small community on the Beaufort coast where I lived for many years, Tbktoyak-tuk, in the Nunatsiaq riding, and then to a nearby town in the Mackenzie Delta, Inuvik.
In Tbktoyaktuk the people told us their town was broke. There were no jobs.
We went next to Inuvik which is in the Western Arctic riding, my riding. We then travelled on to Whitehorse and met with business people, miners, and trappers. From Yukon's capital we went to the capital of the Northwest Territories, Yellowknife, and finally to the southeast comer of my riding, a town at the beginning of the Mackenzie River, Hay River.
All told, the two territories encompass an area of 3.9 million square miles covering 40 per cent of Canada. The two territories are home to 79,000 Canadians living in some 100 communities.
I want to take a few minutes to quote from some of the northerners who made presentations to us about the state of the northern economy. In my mind no one says it as well as the people out there who are carrying the burden of a failing Canadian economy and particularly burdensome in the northern part of Canada where there is an extremely high cost of operating if you are in business, an extremely high cost of living if you are trying to eke out an existence in the rather remote parts of the north.
First of all in the town of Inuvik, Mr. Dick Hill of the Inuvik Chamber of Commerce said:
There is a need for additional northern research support for responsible northern government and organizations so they can collect data and make creative decisions on projects with potential benefits. Effective environmental quality standards need to be set and enforced rather than setting up new commissions to fight projects. Arctic College should be involved to provide objective information collection and analysis. The federal creation of a Polar Commission staffed and based in the south does not make sense to polar residents.
The Hon. Gordon Wray, Minister of Economic Development and Tourism in Yellowknife, said:

There remains a significant requirement, however, for federal investment in infrastructure to ensure the north can realize its vast potential.
Three, the Union of Northern Workers, Jim Evoy, stated:
It is reported that Michael Wilson is considering wage controls in the Federal Public Service. We call on the Liberal Party to oppose such legislation. Wage controls in any sector is exactly the wrong policy to fight the recession and serve only to camouflage the problem. The working people of Canada will not stand idly by and accept the erosion of their income.
In the town of Inuvik, Mayor John Hill stated in regard to grants in lieu of taxes:
If you take a million dollars out of an operation of our size, and yes, that could create bankruptcy. Or it could create a situation where we can't manage our affairs properly. It is unseemly that the federal government should be so irresponsible.
In the community of Hay River, Chris Brodeur stated:
There's no land available for people that want to develop agriculture that requires land, chicken farms require relatively small pieces of land. And we need quotas. And those are two areas directly in the federal government's lap.
He also indicated: "We want the Canadian Coast Guard operations for the western Arctic located in Hay River and not in British Columbia."
Shirley McGrath of the Chamber of Commerce in Yellowknife indicated:
What do we need? Government spending policies that will be supportive of local business without eliminating the competitive element; leadership in actively developing the economy of not only Yellowknife, but of the whole of the NWT; support for selfsustaining industries; opportunities to invest in the north and to keep our money here.
The Dene nation president, Bill Erasmus, said:
My particular membership feels that within our treaty the federal government has a fiduciary responsibility to continue protecting that economy because our people are under the impression that government made the deal with us to continue our way of life.
Last but not least, the Association of Municipalities and the city of Yellowknife under Mayor Pat McMahon indicated:
The Minister of Communications has unilaterally cancelled the public sector rate for municipal radio licences. Simply put, on that day, the federal government decided to levy a massive tax on health and public safety.
A local businessman in Yellowknife, Ron Williams, concluded by saying: "The land claim issue must be resolved so development can take place".

March 6, 1991
Government Orders
These are the things that northerners have indicated to us during our travels into various parts of the north.
There are many issues that northerners feel strongly about; the 24 per cent increase in premiums for unemployment, the cut to the Canadian Jobs Strategy. There is unemployment in the north that reaches the levels of 40 per cent to 60 per cent in some communities.
In relationship to that, we have a subsistence economy of hunting and trapping which has gone down the tubes because the animal rights activists have taken a grip on the whole situation and have turned it into a very brutal public relations campaign against the trappers of Canada. This has had a very detrimental effect.
Any kind of cut in the north, including the Land Use Planning Commission which hurts communities has really been detrimental on the north.
These are the concerns which northerners have. I wish I had more time because there is much more to discuss.

Eventually these provinces will have to turn to the only source of funds they have, the citizens of the province, my constituents. So my constituents still get it in the ear. I asked people to look at this matter very carefully. The question is the deficit that I raised before. People say, "Where are we going to get the money?"
I remember Tommy Douglas, who was a great member of this House for many years, telling me when I first came to the House, he said he was in the House during the Second World War and there was a depression before the war. And the government said, "We can't do anything. We do not have any money". Suddenly the war came and they had to do something. They sure raised the money fast enough. They brought in a fair system of taxation and raised the money.
I am also concerned that we are not looking at bringing in a fair system of taxation. It seems to me that is the way of tackling the deficit. I am afraid that the worst is yet to come. We saw a free trade deal with the United States which is hurting Canadian industry and some Canadian industry is moving south of the border. This is happening in the lower mainland of British Columbia. We are losing some of our manufacturing industry, the little bit that we had.
We are now going to sign a free trade deal with Mexico. That means our workers are going to have to compete with workers who are making $1.25 an hour. You cannot compete with that. So we are going to have more industry moving to the States for cheap labour, where there are bad environmental standards, cheap labour, and exploitation of working people. The government says that there will be better jobs in Canada for Canadians. The problem is that there will be more high-skilled jobs in Canada for which you will have to have more high-skilled people. So what does this budget do? It cuts $100 million out of the Canadian Jobs Strategy program.
Mr. Speaker, I think that is a mistake.
I have heard the Liberal Party in this House be critical of the government, as I have been tonight. But the Liberal Party is a divided party. They always have two positions on every issue. I am proud that in the New Democratic Party we have been very consistent in our attack on the government and in the positions that we have put forward.
Government Orders
So I want to put forward some very positive solutions as to the way I think the government should have acted in the budget.
The first thing we need is a fair system of taxation. Why should a bank teller pay more in taxes than the bank? We still have not cleared that system up. We need a fair system of taxation.
Second, I think we should set goals. We should set goals for deficit reduction. I would like to see it become crystal clear that all of the GST, the Goods and Services Tbc, be put into deficit reduction.
There should be no more frivolous expenditures. I stood up in the House of Commons the other day and asked a question of the Minister of Communications. I asked him why he would put $45 million into a cultural study institute in Montreal. What a waste of money when when no one wanted it. And I am pleased to see that the government eventually backed down. It is this kind of expenditure that is making the government look bad and is so wasteful.
Third, we have to clean up our constitutional position in this country, the stalemate. Let's get this over. Let's make a decision: either Quebec stays or goes. We get a new constitutional position in shape and we tackle what really matters to this country, and that is the future.
Finally, I think that a smart government would invest in education, would invest in health, would invest in the environment. These are the great investments. Common sense dictates that. The people in my area have a lot of common sense, and if they were here tonight in the House of Commons that is what they would be telling the government. And I am pleased to do that on their behalf.
