Mr. Speaker, tonight we are here to debate Bill C-97, which is an Act to provide borrowing authority. Of course, Bill C-97 is inexorably intertwined with the budget, as has been so often said by so many speakers.
Bill C-97 asks this House to allow the government to borrow $26.4 billion. Where does that figure come from? The Finance Minister and the government have come up with that figure based on certain assumptions. Those assumptions are stated in the budget, and they are assumed to be correct.

Government Orders
The Tories take delight in reviewing history whenever they talk about the Liberal Party and in reminding us about their revisionist view of what the Liberals did. Well, this is dreamland. I want to talk about facts. So, I am going to ask us to go back factually and examine how the Finance Minister's assumptions have fared-factually, not fancifully.
Let's go back to November 8, 1984 when the Finance Minister delivered an economic statement. At that time he promised "to put our fiscal house in order so that we can reverse the massive build-up in public debt".
Mr. Speaker, he was wrong. The debt has ballooned from $168 billion to almost $400 billion in the six years that he has been Finance Minister. He predicted then that in the 1984-85 fiscal year the deficit would be $34.5 billion. He was wrong.
Seven months after that prediction, which was wrong, he admitted it was wrong. He announced in the budget of May 23, 1985, his first budget, that the deficit would be, not $34.6 billion, but rather $36 billion. Speaking of where to find additional revenue, he said, and I quote:
Ultimately, we would be forced to find money through drastic cuts in government services and major tax increases. Many government programs would be in jeopardy. This is also unacceptable.
Mr. Speaker, can you believe it? This is the finance minister saying on May 23, 1985, that it is unacceptable to him to have drastic cuts in government services and major tax increases. Yet, what did he do? In fact, he cut government services. The government is now out of the unemployment insurance plan. He cut VIA. He gutted the CBC and he has imposed the most massive tax grab in Canadian history, the GST.
February 26, 1986, along came the second budget, and what does he say? I quote:
This budget will reduce the deficit to $29.8 billion in the coming fiscal year and by the end of the decade it will be cut to $22 billion.
He was wrong, because last week he said, not $22 billion but $30.5 billion.
He said, and I quote:
Our national debt will no longer be growing faster than the economy.
He was wrong.
The federal debt as a percentage of Gross Domestic Product has risen from a debt equalling 46.4 per cent of the Gross Domestic Product to a debt equalling 57.3 per cent of the GDP in 1990-1991. This is an astounding 10.9 per cent increase and while doing this 10.9 per cent increase, totally contrary to his predictions, he has driven us into a made-in-Ottawa recession. He said, and I quote:
The amount we must borrow each year to pay the bills will be cut
from 28.3 billion in 1985-1986 to $17.9 billion in 1987-1988.
He was wrong. Today we are talking about Bill C-97 where he is asking us to borrow, not $17.9 billion, but $26.4 billion.
February 18, 1987, his third budget, and I quote:
I am also announcing today that in our third year we will get the
deficit down to $29.3 billion.
He was wrong.
In his seventh year as finance minister, it is not $29.3 billion. No. It is $30.5 billion.
February 10, 1988, the fourth budget, and I quote:
For the current fiscal year, I said we would cut the deficit to $29.3
billion. We will meet that target.
Current-he is talking about 1988-1989. He was wrong. He repeated the same thing two years in a row, and both years he was wrong and he is still wrong today.
April 27, 1989, the fifth budget, speaking about the debt, and I quote:
It is now more than $320 billion.
This was a rise of $152 billion more than when he gave his economic statement back in 1984. In five years, there was a $152 billion increase in the national debt. The government is not reducing the debt. It continues to balloon.
Speaking of the deficit, he predicted that he would, and I quote:
-reduce the annual deficit to $30.5 billion. Next year, it will be
reduced to $28 billion.
He was wrong. Do not forget that in his second budget in 1986, he predicted that the deficit would be $22 billion. In his fifth budget, he revised it to $30.5 billion and he was wrong. He then said that the year after it would be $28 billion. We know he was wrong.

February 20, 1990, the sixth budget of this finance minister. What did he say? I quote:
We will reduce the deficit to $28.5 billion this fiscal year. We will
cut it in half to $14 billion in three more years. And we will reduce it
further to $10 billion in the year after that.
He was wrong. Today, by his own admission, it is $30.5 billion. It will not be $14 billion in 1993, as he predicted because he knows he was wrong. In his present budget, he predicts it is going to be $25 billion.
In that sixth budget, he said the following, and I quote:
- the debt is still growing faster than the economy-faster than our ability to pay.
This surely is proof of his inability, since in all his previous budgets he assured Canadians that he would reduce growth of debt to less than the growth of the economy. Yet, he admitted the debt was growing faster than the economy.
We turn to the seventh budget. He has been consistently wrong for one economic statement and six budgets. Quite an unimpressive track record. This is despite 33 separate tax increases, despite imposing the GST, despite the fact, or perhaps because of the fact that wealthy Canadians are paying less tax than in 1984 while middle and lower income Canadians are paying more tax.
With this type of record, only two things are certain. First, the minister's budgetary predictions will be wrong again. Second, lower and middle income Canadians will continue to pay higher taxes to a government that has been consistently wrong in its fiscal and economic projections.
Finally, a Minister of Finance who has had seven chances and has consistently failed to achieve his objectives should do the honourable thing: resign.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take the opportunity today to be able to speak on Bill C-97, the borrowing authority bill.
This bill flows directly from the Minister of Finance's budget delivered on February 26 of this year. The government's budget, the seventh of this administration, is yet another crystal-ball budget with the Minister of Finance as the fortune-teller for Canada.
Government Orders
This budget and the past six budgets make future promises and blames current failures on previous governments, but neglects to reflect on past budget deficiencies, of which there have been many, many, many.
How does this occur? Well, let us review. Let us reflect upon the promises and predictions of the past. In 1985, the Minister of Finance predicted an $18 billion deficit in 1991. Now, it is $30.5 billion. He predicted $18.5 billion, he delivered $30 billion more deficit.
In 1984, the Prime Minister promised jobs, jobs, jobs. Today, 1.3 million Canadians are unemployed and soon, by government figures, 1.5 million or 10 per cent of our work force will be unemployed.
Last year, the finance minister forecast 11 per cent interest rates, but the rates still remained at 13 per cent. When first elected this government set certain priorities. The debt, the deficit and the economy were the highest priorities of this government. Tbday the deficit is still $30 billion annually. The debt has well over doubled to $400 billion and the economy is in a recession. Boy, have they delivered on their highest priorities in their years in government. So much for reflections of the past.
Let us say today what are the priorities in this country. I think anyone who is looking at Canada certainly realizes the recession has to be number one. We all realize national unity is certainly among the top priorities. And the problem the government has struggled with for so many years, the debt is twice as bad as it was when they came in.
But does this budget deal with those priorities in any substantial way? Has it done anything to help the farmers, the business people, the people that I see daily in southwestern Ontario? I do not see anything there. Does it do much to help national unity? We have heard person after person rise in this House and talk about the difficulties, the cutting of all of our programs, freezing, restraining, shifting burdens to the provinces, cutting Canadian Jobs Strategy, cutting social housing. We have heard that, one after the other, after the other.
This government is shifting a financial burden from itself to the provinces and municipalities. What is the reasoning it uses? Very clearly it said: "They don't owe as much as we do, therefore they should pick up a bigger portion". I think that is pretty weak logic when you stop and consider the builders of the debt and deficit were the Tbries. They doubled it. They promised, and promised,

Government Orders
and promised a reduced deficit but delivered a deficit of $30 billion consistently for seven years. They have not been innovative. Their policies are hampering the national government in dealing with national issues, dealing with national institutions, such as health care, education, training, safety nets.
We are being criticized by many in this country who are saying possibly programs should be delivered at the provincial level. We are splitting in this country over some of these values and yet our federal government in this last budget is negating its responsibility for many of the programs which hold our nation together.
We must look to what is happening, not put our heads in the sand and say: "We'll reduce the debt. A crystal ball will make that happen for us". This government continues to blame past governments for its failures. Seven years of putting budgets together should bring IT to the reality that the problems are its own. This government has caused this recession. This government has caused high interest rates. This government has caused the negative effects of the high Canadian dollar and has caused today's dilemmas.
We heard not six months ago the Minister of Finance bragging about how he kept the dollar rate up to fight inflation. He was warned at that time he would drive us to a recession but he did not heed the warnings. He put us in a recession. He said he was cooling the economy off. We said he was driving us to a recession. His crystal ball is broken.
The government has made predictions for the future. Are they to be believed? Their past track record says no. Yet, the government wants Canadians to believe in these facts, in 2 per cent inflation in this country. We almost did that 2 per cent in one month of this year and yet it is predicting 2 per cent inflation shortly down the line.
They want us to believe that we will lower our interest rates. Well, we have followed very clearly the lowering of interest rates in the United States. Canada has not independently moved beyond that. Canada has only followed the U.S. and the difference in interest rates remains very steady, 4 per cent to 5 per cent difference between Canada and the United States.
The government has said job creation is a high priority and yet it has cut, cut, cut. It said we would have a good economy, but look what it has done to our economy at this point. The businesses that are leaving Canada today will not be returning. Canadians' memories are not that short. Canadians will remember that these are the same things the finance minister has said for seven years: all good things will come; the economy will improve; the deficit will be lowered. Consistently saying it.
Canadians now realize he did not have workable plans. He could not see into the future and he certainly led us down a terrible pathway. The scenario that the Conservative governments are better managers than other governments is totally unacceptable. Every year we are told the next year will be better. Every year we hear the next year the deficit will come down. The fact is, the next years have come and gone and the predictions never come true.
In 1984 the government revenue was $70.9 billion. Today it is $128 billion, an increase in taxes of $57 billion or 81.2 per cent. Yet the deficit still remains at $30 billion. Annually the government revenues have increased more than inflation. Still we have a huge deficit, a huge debt, doubled. The public debt as a percentage of the gross national product is growing. The interest charges on the debt have grown slower than the increases in revenues. No matter how you calculate it, seven years of growth, 81 per cent higher income taxes, yet more than double the debt from $168 billion in the second half of 1984, to its point today, $411 billion. It has not dealt with the major issues in this country. I think every Canadian deserves a better role than has been issued to them today.

Mr. Speaker, just a couple of words. I certainly will not require 10 minutes in the closing moments of this debate on the borrowing authority.
I would like to point out two things relating to the borrowing authority and the federal budget, two points that have not been made by anybody, have not been mentioned by the news media and certainly not mentioned by the Government of Canada.
The first point is a rather technical point. I was looking a few moments ago at the fiscal equalization payments for this year. Mr. Speaker, I noticed that your province
March 6, 1991

will be getting a big zero in fiscal equalization because, of course, your province does not receive any funding. The people of British Columbia do not receive any money. Ontario also receives zero. That is to be expected because the formula is based upon the ability of a province to raise revenues through taxation, as you know.
Then when I looked at the other provinces, I looked at Saskatchewan and it is up to over $500 million. Manitoba, coming east, is up to over $900 million. It is increasing this year coming up. And then I looked at Quebec and it is increasing by $53.7 million, up to $3,886 billion.
Then I came to what we regard as being the poorer provinces of Canada, and I noticed that New Brunswick was up $26 million. That is interesting, just $26 million. I noticed that Nova Scotia is up $22.1 million, a little bit less. I noticed that Prince Edward Island is up $4.2 million. Now we are really getting down, are we not, to zero? Then we come to the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that it is receiving-and these are the official figures from the Department of Finance-less $16.9 million less than it received last year.
We hear speakers in this Chamber, the Minister of Finance, the President of the Treasury Board, the Prime Minister and other members say: "Well, there wasn't really a cut. There was a less than normal increase in these equalization payments". I do not want to give the impression that they were telling fibs, because in fact they were not.
When I look a little bit closer I discover that the federal government is subtracting moneys that are owed by these provinces, it claims, from three years ago. In fact the federal government, according to its audit which was done in January, said that those governments received more money than they should have received back in 1987, 1988 and 1989.
I make this point simply because in our estimates of expenditure we forgive moneys that are owed by foreign banks to the Government of Canada. We forgive moneys that are owed by foreign nations to the Government of Canada. But this government will not forgive money owed by our developing provinces of Canada.
Government Orders
The Newfoundland government is presenting a budget tomorrow afternoon at three o'clock. You can imagine, Mr. Speaker, the attention on that budget tomorrow with these equalization payments to the Government of Newfoundland actually decreasing over last year. Imagine, tomorrow the attention of Newfoundlanders will be riveted on one channel to the budget and probably on the other channel to the Brier in Hamilton, because we have an excellent team there headed by a young fellow, John Boland, who I think is going to become victorious on the weekend.
Between our learned premier, our excellent premier, and our excellent John Boland curling team, we will probably hear a not so excellent budget in the background, delivered by Dr. Kitchen, Ph.D. Next to him is Dr. Gibbons, Ph.D. Next to him is Dr. Warren, Ph.D. I think we have more Ph.D.s in the Newfoundland government than in any provincial government in the history of Canada.
But no matter how learned you are or what a great economist you are, you cannot create something out of negative figures. That is point number one. Point number two is this: I examined the cuts to the departments and I found one interesting thing. We are all politicians in this Chamber, but sometimes-and I looked for this specifically and I found it this morning-I wonder where were the politics in these cuts. I went through the figures and I verified them after with the Department of Finance.
I saw every major development fund cut in this country. ACOA is cut in eastern Canada. The Western Canadian Diversification Fund is cut in western Canada, but the Quebec Development Fund is up $20 million.
The minister in charge of that is of course the minister of industry and it is his decision to make. But I challenge the minister to explain to the Canadian public tomorrow why that fund went up $20 million and every single other development fund in this country actually went down by more than that figure.
Those are two points in government reductions. I can guarantee that that does not do anything for Canadian unity. That does nothing for Canadian unity.

I notice that the press did not pick it up and members did not pick it up. Maybe nothing else will be said of it. But I am going to ask the minister tomorrow to take this transcript and to say something to the members of the House of Commons as to why he used his ministerial authority to override Treasury Board and to transplant an enormous increase into the one major fund and cut the other two major funds in this country.
I say that it is not all as clear as it seems, as it is presented by the Government of Canada. Sometimes we have to look between the lines and we have to ask a lot of questions. And we discover that the Government of Canada has not been forthright. It has not come forward and presented what it has done.
Mr. Speaker, I see that my time is up. I trust that these few words were interesting to you.
